## Multi-agent systems for scholarly production

Agent systems already automate parts of scholarly production, including writing scientific surveys and checking that citations support the claims they are attached to [@yang2026deepsurvey]. DeepSurvey is a direct example. It extracts structured keynotes and models relationships across papers through clustering and comparative analysis. It also recovers implementation-level details with a code-agent subsystem. For reliability, it expands the citation graph with hybrid filtering for topic-focused retrieval and constrains analysis and writing to evidence. It then runs agentic refinement at several granularities to validate that each citation aligns with its claim [@yang2026deepsurvey].

Galley shares this concern with citation reliability but differs in scope and in where it places the check. DeepSurvey generates surveys. Galley takes a seed, the text a person supplies, and carries it through impact review, planning, drafting, peer review and closing reconciliation (Sections 4 to 6). Its citation check starts with a code test that comes before any model judgment. Code first confirms that the supporting passage is copied verbatim from the cited work's abstract. Only then does a model family other than the one that proposed the passage judge whether the passage supports the claim.

## Provenance in AI-assisted writing

Provenance for AI-assisted writing is a second concern. We expect that interactive provenance visualization can show authors which parts of a text an LLM contributed. Galley records provenance at the level of claims and decisions rather than authorship of text. Each manuscript ends with two records. The first is a claim ledger that lists every claim with its kind, its standing, whether the seed or the system made it, and its sources. The second is a production record generated from the run's production journal. The run also writes a sign-off sheet of what only the authors can decide and an evidence package of claims, evidence and sources in the Resolvent format (Section 8).

## Fabricated citations

LLM-generated scholarly text can contain misattributed citations. A systematic review of hallucinations in academic contexts identified six recurring types and found fabricated or inaccurate citations to be the most prevalent [@lai2026hallucinatio]. Another study examined LLM-generated literature reviews in mental health. It evaluated 333 citation-claims against their cited sources and found that 19.8% were fabrications, 18.3% contained major errors, 18.3% contained minor errors and 43.5% were accurate [@linardon2026fluency]. These findings make citation support something to check on every citation rather than assume. They motivate Galley's verbatim match and its three-outcome verification (Section 5).

## Self-preference in LLM evaluators

LLMs used as evaluators tend to rate their own outputs more favorably than outputs from other models. Panickssery et al. describe self-preference as an LLM evaluator scoring its own outputs higher than others' outputs even when human annotators judge them to be of equal quality [@panickssery2024llm]. Chen et al. report that LLMs serving as judges tend to favor their own responses over those generated by other models [@chen2025beyond]. Suppose a multi-agent pipeline has one model draft a text and the same model review it under another prompt. That pipeline places the model where these studies place their evaluators: judging its own output.

Galley responds to this evidence structurally. It assigns every evaluating seat to a model family other than the producing one. As a result, no family selects among its own reformulations, verifies its own citations, judges its own referee responses, adjudicates its own disputes or reconciles its own final manuscript (Section 3).

## Separation of duties and fault seeding

Separation of duties is a security principle that organizations have used extensively to prevent conflict of interest, fraud and error [@kugblenu2007separation]. Galley applies the principle to model families instead of people. The family that produces an output does not hold the seat that evaluates it, and code enforces this assignment, not a prompt.

Fault seeding is the second practice Galley adapts. In software testing, planting known defects and counting how many are detected is an established way to estimate how sensitive a test suite is. Testers commonly seed faults by hand or with a program that generates mutants from a set of mutation operators. The generated form allows systematic, repeatable seeding of many faults for statistical analysis [@andrews2006using]. Mutation testing is a well-established technique for evaluating a test suite by the extent to which it detects injected faults [@ma2018deepmutation]. The same literature records that it is not known whether results obtained from generated faults lead to valid, representative conclusions [@andrews2006using].

The `calibrate` behavior applies fault seeding to a model instead of a test suite. Among the verified citations of the manuscript in hand, it places planted defects and unaltered controls. It then measures how many planted defects the verifier rejects and how many controls the verifier accepts (Section 7).

## The gap

We hypothesize that prior multi-agent scholarly systems assign drafting, reviewing and verifying roles through prompts. We further hypothesize that they state no rule requiring the evaluating model to come from a different model family than the model that produced the work. If that holds, nothing in such a system prevents one family from producing a passage and then judging it. That is the configuration in which self-preference has been measured [@panickssery2024llm; @chen2025beyond].

Cross-family separation of duties is designed to close this gap with a rule enforced in code. It joins three strands that the work above treats separately: the principle of separating duties to prevent conflict of interest and error, the evidence that LLM evaluators favor their own outputs, and the practice of measuring a checker's sensitivity with planted defects. Section 3 defines the rule and the five decisions it governs.

S4.text:
Galley breaks the production of a manuscript, from seed to submission, into a ladder of 27 atomic behaviors. The seed is the only input a person must supply. Every later step, from reading the seed to marking the paper ready, is the work of one of these behaviors.

## Atomic behaviors

An atomic behavior is a unit of work that reads the paper's state, does one thing and writes its result. It does not know which behavior runs next.

We carried this design over from our earlier system, `autonomio/poise`, which we built for semi-autonomous software engineering. Galley applies the same design to a scholarly manuscript. Each unit of work stays small, and the order of work belongs to the scheduler, not to any behavior.

## The ladder and the scheduler

The ladder is the ordered list of the 27 atomic behaviors, in scan order: (1) `extract`, (2) `position`, (3) `review-idea`, (4) `reformulate`, (5) `select-direction`, (6) `literature-review`, (7) `analyze`, (8) `simulate`, (9) `plan`, (10) `outline`, (11) `find-evidence`, (12) `verify`, (13) `reassess`, (14) `calibrate`, (15) `draft`, (16) `figure`, (17) `fidelity`, (18) `frame`, (19) `referee`, (20) `close-round`, (21) `respond`, (22) `verify-disposition`, (23) `adjudicate`, (24) `reconcile`, (25) `reprofile`, (26) `typeset` and (27) `ready`. The scheduler scans the ladder from the top, runs whatever is ready, and scans again from the top whenever any behavior settles. Readiness, which the scheduler checks against the paper's state on each scan, decides whether a behavior runs, and position on the ladder decides which ready behavior a scan reaches first. After a behavior settles, the next scan can run a ready behavior higher on the ladder. When `respond` (21) answers a finding with a new claim that needs evidence, `find-evidence` (11) and `verify` (12) take that claim up before the author answers again, and no behavior needs to know that it must loop.

## Skeleton behaviors and improvers

Minor issues do not block work. Only the seven skeleton behaviors are required for a paper to exist: `extract` (1), `plan` (9), `outline` (10), `draft` (15), `frame` (18), `typeset` (26) and `ready` (27). The other twenty behaviors are improvers. An improver can make the paper better but cannot stop it, so small defects do not halt production.

## Isolated steps and the production journal

Each model family runs through its own command-line client with no tools and no delegation, and it answers in a strict JSON schema. Inside the step, the model does not search, run code or hand work to another agent.

Galley stores every prompt and answer in the paper's folder. We call this stored record the production journal. A rerun takes each model's answer from the journal instead of calling the model. The journal lets a reader inspect the run's recorded prompts and answers and replay its model exchanges step by step.

## Building the ladder one behavior at a time

We built the behaviors one at a time and showed each one working before we built the next. We continued until the chain of 27 behaviors covered the whole path from seed to submission.

revisions.text:
Galley breaks the production of a manuscript, from seed to submission, into a ladder of 27 atomic behaviors. The seed is the only input a person must supply. Every later step, from reading the seed to marking the paper ready, is the work of one of these behaviors. This section describes the unit of work and the scheduler that decides what runs. It then covers the split between required and optional behaviors and the way each behavior calls a model. Figure 2 shows the ladder in scan order.

## Atomic behaviors

An atomic behavior is a unit of work that reads the paper's state, does one thing and writes its result. It does not know which behavior runs next. Its only link to other behaviors is the state they all read and write. One line therefore describes each behavior: `extract` reads the seed and lists its claims, `verify` judges one candidate passage against its claim, and `typeset` renders the manuscript whenever the text changes.

We carried this design over from our earlier system, `autonomio/poise`, which we built for semi-autonomous software engineering. Galley applies the same design to a scholarly manuscript. Each unit of work stays small, and the order of work belongs to the scheduler, not to any behavior.

## The ladder and the scheduler

The ladder is the ordered list of the 27 atomic behaviors. The scheduler scans the ladder from the top, runs whatever is ready, and scans again from the top whenever any behavior settles. Readiness decides whether a behavior runs. Position on the ladder decides which ready behavior a scan reaches first.

Galley stores no fixed sequence of steps. The path through the ladder follows from the paper's state at each scan. A scan passes over a behavior that is not ready, and a later scan reaches it again once the behaviors it depends on have written their results. For example, `draft` writes a section only once that section's evidence is settled.

Because every scan starts at the top, a result written low on the ladder can make a behavior higher up ready again. Suppose the author answers a referee finding with "needs evidence." The new claim then goes through search and verification, which sit above the referee behaviors, before the author answers again. Likewise, when the text changes, `typeset` renders it again. These returns follow from the scheduler's rule that every settlement starts a new scan from behavior 1. No behavior needs to know that it must loop.

## Skeleton behaviors and improvers

Minor issues do not block work. Only the seven skeleton behaviors are required for a paper to exist: `extract`, `plan`, `outline`, `draft`, `frame`, `typeset` and `ready`. Every other behavior is an improver. An improver can make the paper better but cannot stop it, so small defects do not halt production.

The split separates two questions: whether a paper exists, and how good it is. The skeleton answers the first. It reads the seed, sets the thesis and the claim graph, lays out the sections and drafts them. It then frames the title and abstract, typesets the result and marks it ready for submission. The improvers answer the second question. They place the idea among prior work, score it against the seven-factor impact standard, and find and verify evidence. They also run peer review and reconcile the final text against the claim ledger. Sections 5 to 7 describe these improvers. In Figure 2, solid boxes mark the skeleton and dashed boxes mark the improvers.

## Isolated steps and the production journal

Each model family runs through its own command-line client with no tools and no delegation, and it answers in a strict JSON schema. A model step is therefore a single exchange. The behavior builds a prompt from the paper's state, the family in the seat answers in the schema, and the behavior writes the result. Inside the step, the model does not search, run code or hand work to another agent. Literature searches, analyses and simulations run in Galley's own code, outside the model's step.

Every prompt and every answer is stored in the paper's folder. We call this stored record the production journal. A rerun replays the journal without calling a model, so anyone can audit a run and reproduce it step by step. Because each atomic behavior does one thing, the journal reads as a series of single decisions. Each decision sits with the prompt that asked for it and the answer that settled it.

Isolation also preserves the record of who decided what. Each family answers through its own client, so every answer in the journal comes from one known family in one seat. Under cross-family separation of duties (Section 3), the journal therefore shows, for each judgment, which family produced the work and which family judged it.

## Building the ladder one behavior at a time

We built the behaviors one at a time and showed each one working before we built the next. We continued until the chain of 27 behaviors covered the whole path from seed to submission. The atomic design suits this way of building. A behavior that reads state and writes a result can be run and inspected on its own, before any behavior that uses its result exists. No behavior already on the ladder needs to know about a new one, because none of them knows what comes next. Figure 2 shows the chain this process produced.

S6.text:
In Galley, referees from different model families review the manuscript. Reconciliation follows peer review. Cross-family separation of duties decides who judges at each step. The author writes the text and answers material findings. Another model family judges both the text and the answers.

## Referee seats and findings

Four referee seats review the manuscript: methods, the host field, citations and the desk editor. Each seat comes from a model family other than the author's. The families rotate between rounds, so a seat held by one family in a round passes to another family in the next.

Each seat can raise findings. A finding names an issue in the manuscript and carries a severity.

## Answers and their judgment

The author answers each material finding with one of four dispositions. A fix lists the exact edits made to the text. A rebuttal argues that the finding does not hold. A limitation accepts the finding and states it as a limitation of the work. The author can also request new evidence on the finding.

The referee who raised a finding judges the answer to it. The family that wrote an answer never decides whether that answer settles the finding.

The evaluated run allowed up to three author answers per finding. A finding still disputed at that cap goes to adjudication by a family distinct from both the author's and the raising referee's.

The evaluated run allowed at most two referee rounds. The production journal stores every finding, answer, judgment and adjudication from the run.

## Closing reconciliation

Review can change the text and leave the claim ledger out of step with it. A fix can soften a sentence. A limitation can qualify a claim. An edit in one section can remove a statement that the ledger still lists. When this happens, the ledger records claims at a strength the text no longer gives them.

Closing reconciliation checks the claim ledger against the post-review text. Once peer review finishes, a family other than the author's reads the final text against every claim in the claim ledger and assigns each claim one of three outcomes. It confirms a claim that the text still states as recorded. It narrows a claim to the text's wording when the text now says less than the ledger. It drops a claim that the text no longer states. The production journal stores each outcome with the claim it applies to. Because reconciliation follows peer review and adjudication, referees read the pre-reconciliation ledger, and the typeset step renders the reconciled ledger, evidence package and sign-off sheet only after review ends.

Reconciliation aligns recorded claims with the text through a cross-family model judgment, and the typeset step propagates the resulting ledger across the companion artifacts. Reconciliation works from the recorded claims and updates the ledger rather than the text, so an assertion that never entered the ledger lies outside its check. The reconciling family's judgment decides which recorded claims remain in the ledger and how the ledger states them. Claims that reconciliation drops do not appear in the appended ledger, the evidence package or the sign-off sheet. When the text or ledger changes, the typeset step renders the manuscript with its appended ledger, the evidence package and the sign-off sheet from the same revision. Those three outputs therefore carry the same claim entries by derivation from one revision rather than by a comparison after rendering. The ready step marks the paper ready for submission only once every gate holds on one revision. Code enforces the cross-family seat assignment for reconciliation, while claim-to-text agreement on recorded claims rests on that family's judgment rather than a code check.

In Galley, review is a set of atomic behaviors that act on a complete manuscript: `referee`, `close-round`, `respond`, `verify-disposition` and `adjudicate`, followed by `reconcile` once review ends. Cross-family separation of duties decides who judges at each step. The author seat writes the text and answers for it. Another model family judges both the text and the answers.

## Referee seats and findings

Four referee seats review the whole manuscript: methods, the host field, citations and the desk editor. Each seat comes from a model family other than the author's. The families rotate between rounds, so a seat held by one family in a round passes to another family in the next. In the evaluated run, Claude Opus 5.5 held the author seat. Every referee seat therefore came from either the GPT-6.2 Sol family or the Gemini 4 Carbon family.

Each seat raises findings. A finding names an issue in the manuscript, carries a severity and states the decision it asks for. `close-round` ends a round once every seat has reported. The author then answers the round's findings as one set.

## Answers and their judgment

The author answers each material finding with one of four dispositions. A fix lists the exact edits made to the text. A rebuttal argues that the finding does not hold. A limitation accepts the finding and states it as a limitation of the work. A request for evidence turns the finding into a new claim. That claim goes through search and verification before the author answers again.

The referee who raised a finding judges the answer to it through `verify-disposition`. The family that wrote an answer never decides whether that answer settles the finding. The decision stays with the family that raised the concern.

When the referee rejects an answer, the author may answer again, up to a cap on answers per finding. The evaluated run set this cap at 3 answers per finding. A finding still disputed at the cap goes to `adjudicate`. The adjudicator is the family that is neither the author's nor the referee's. With three model families, this is always the one family not yet party to the dispute. The sign-off sheet lists every decision a third family made, so the authors see each finding that the author and the referee did not settle between themselves.

The evaluated run used 2 referee rounds. The production journal stores every finding, answer, judgment and adjudication, so a rerun replays the whole review without calling a model. The production record generated from this journal reports the counts of findings, resolutions and adjudications, and the evaluation section gives them.

## Closing reconciliation

Review changes the text, and the claim ledger can then fall out of step with it. A fix can soften a sentence. A limitation can qualify a claim. An edit in one section can remove a statement that the ledger still lists. When this happens, the ledger records claims at a strength the text no longer gives them.

`reconcile` corrects this mismatch. Once review is finished, a family other than the author's reads the final text against every claim in the claim ledger and assigns each claim one of three outcomes. It confirms a claim that the text still states as recorded. It narrows a claim to the text's wording when the text now says less than the ledger. It drops a claim that the text no longer states.

After reconciliation, the claim ledger, the evidence package in the Resolvent format and the sign-off sheet say what the manuscript says. A claim in the ledger appears in the text at the strength the ledger records. A claim the text no longer makes does not appear among the items the authors are asked to sign off. The family that wrote the final text does not certify that the ledger matches it. The cross-family rule governs this closing check just as it governs citation verification, the judgment of answers and adjudication.

Reconciliation works from the recorded claims and updates the ledger rather than the text, so an assertion that never entered the ledger lies outside its check. The reconciling family's judgment decides which recorded claims remain in the ledger and how the ledger states them. Claims that reconciliation drops do not appear in the appended ledger, the evidence package or the sign-off sheet. When the text or ledger changes, the typeset step renders the manuscript with its appended ledger, the evidence package and the sign-off sheet from the same revision. Those three outputs therefore carry the same claim entries by derivation from one revision rather than by a comparison after rendering. The ready step marks the paper ready for submission only once every gate holds on one revision. Code enforces the cross-family seat assignment for reconciliation, while claim-to-text agreement on recorded claims rests on that family's judgment rather than a code check.

## Impact interrogation and reformulation

Before it writes any text, Galley screens the seed against a seven-factor impact standard, the authors' own design heuristic for how the paper should be written. Galley scores the seed on each factor, names the weakest factor and returns one of three verdicts: worth writing, reformulate, or no contribution. Like every improver, this screen can redirect the paper but cannot stop it. The same seven factors score the finished paper again. 

A reformulate verdict leads to exactly three directions. Galley proposes them. Each direction differs structurally from the other two, and each keeps the seed's explicit commitments.  Galley then chooses either the original idea or one of the three directions. A family other than the proposing family makes this choice. 

## Filling the gaps the argument needs

Once Galley selects a direction, it addresses gaps in the argument. Evidence search is the main route. Two further routes are optional, and both run on the authors' machine.

Galley can analyze the authors' data on their machine.  Galley can also run a simulation on the authors' machine.  

## Evidence search through Canary

Galley finds external evidence through Canary, the component it uses to search OpenAlex, a fully open index of scholarly works, authors, venues and institutions [@priem2022openalex; @priem2024openalex]. Galley's source, including its calls to Canary, is released under the MIT licence at https://github.com/autonomio/galley.   For each claim that needs external evidence, Galley writes search queries, runs them through Canary and considers up to a set number of candidate works. The run used a cap of 10 candidate works per claim. 

At the authors' request, Canary also reviews the literature in the background, in what we call a model-run review. The author writes a review question. A research model plans the search of OpenAlex, screens the candidates, reads their full texts and quotes the passage behind each finding, and an independent model audits every finding. Each upheld finding joins the claim ledger and the evidence package with its quoted passage as a verified citation. A reader audits a model-run review finding by finding, against each finding's quoted passage and its independent audit.

## Verbatim-gated citation verification

For citations from claim-level evidence search, Galley checks candidate works against abstracts only and accepts a citation only when code confirms that the supporting passage is copied verbatim from the cited work's abstract. Citations from a model-run review rest instead on full-text passages that an independent model has audited.  

Two families also act on each citation from claim-level evidence search. The checker proposes a passage for a claim. The verifier belongs to a different family and judges the passage against that claim. Such a citation thus needs both a verbatim match confirmed by code and a judgment of support from the verifier. The verifier classifies each passage as supported, narrower or not supported. A supported passage keeps the claim and the citation as they stand. A narrower passage keeps the citation and narrows the claim to what the passage states. Galley rejects a citation judged not supported.

Galley takes the bibliographic record for a cited work with a DOI from the DOI registry.  

## Claims without evidence

Galley writes claims without evidence as hypotheses. Two behaviors check the thesis and the prose against the available evidence.

A load-bearing claim is one the thesis depends on. When such a claim ends without evidence, the `reassess` behavior decides whether the thesis stands, narrows or fails. The `fidelity` behavior rewrites drafted sentences that say more than their evidence supports.

## Impact interrogation and reformulation

The verdict comes before drafting, so it can change what the paper argues and not only how the paper words it.

A reformulate verdict leads to exactly three directions. The `reformulate` behavior proposes them. This is the first decision that cross-family separation of duties governs (Section 3).

Once the direction is settled, Galley fills the gaps the argument needs. Evidence search is the main route. Two further routes are optional, and both run on the authors' machine.

S8.text:
## Joining a run

Galley lets a person join a run at any point and never requires one to.  

A person can edit the manuscript directly in the editor. Galley treats those edits as the person's revision and takes them up on the next run. 

A comment in the editor becomes a thread. By default, the agents take over the thread. A person who marks the thread `@humans` keeps it for themselves. A person who marks it `@both` shares it with the agents.

In an `@both` thread, the agents' edits arrive as proposed changes. Each proposed change is marked at its place in the document, and the person accepts or declines it.  

Citation choices give a person control over which sources the paper cites. With citation choices turned on, each claim waits for the person's decision. The person can select candidate source a, b or c, let Galley choose, or state the claim without a source.  This run used automatic citation.

The dial sets which steps wait for a person. Its `autonomous` setting lets every step proceed without waiting for a person, while leaving human edits and comment threads optional. Another setting makes load-bearing citations and critical answers wait for the person. A further setting makes every answer wait for the person. 

## Provenance each run leaves

Every manuscript Galley produces includes a claim ledger at the end. For each claim the run records, the ledger gives its kind, its standing, its origin (the seed or the system) and its sources.

Each manuscript also carries a production record generated from the run's production journal.  

The run writes a sign-off sheet alongside the manuscript. The sheet lists what only the authors can decide: the declarations, the claims the system added, the claims stated as hypotheses, the decisions a third family made, and the steps that were skipped. 

Each run also writes its own evidence package through the typeset behavior, implemented in Galley's open-source repository (https://github.com/autonomio/galley). The package holds the paper's claims, evidence and sources in the Resolvent format. Digital-library research may already model provenance at the level of individual claims, holding each assertion, its evidence and its source as one machine-readable record; how the Resolvent format relates to such models remains an open question. The evidence for a cited claim is the passage that code confirmed is copied verbatim from the cited work's abstract and that the verifier judged. A cited work with a DOI takes its bibliographic record from the DOI registry. After peer review, a family other than the author's reconciles the recorded claims in the ledger against the final text, and the typeset behavior writes the package from that reconciled state (Section 6).

The claim ledger and the production record appear in the manuscript itself. The sign-off sheet, the evidence package and the production journal are written to the paper's folder. Galley does not publish them, so readers can inspect a run's files only where its authors release that folder. The journal stores every prompt and answer of the run. For each candidate citation it holds the verifier's prompt, with the claim and the passage exactly as the verifier received them, and the verifier's judgment. A rerun replays the journal without calling a model.

revisions.text:
## Joining a run

Galley lets a person join a run at any point and never requires one to. The seed is the only input a person must supply. Every other point of contact described below is optional, and each one is a choice the person makes, not a condition the run waits on by default.

A person can edit the manuscript directly in the editor. Galley treats those edits as the person's revision and takes them up on the next run. The atomic behaviors that run afterward read the edited text as the paper's current state, so the person's wording becomes the text the agents work from.

A comment in the editor becomes a thread. By default, the agents take the thread over and act on it. A person who marks the thread `@humans` keeps it for themselves. A person who marks it `@both` shares it with the agents.

In an `@both` thread, the agents' edits arrive as proposed changes. Each proposed change is marked at its place in the document, and the person accepts or declines it. The person therefore decides, one edit at a time, which agent edits enter the text. We present this mechanism as a design; it has not been tested with users.

Citation choices give a person control over which sources the paper cites. With citation choices turned on, each claim waits for the person to do one of three things: pick one of its candidate sources, labeled a, b and c; let the system pick; or state the claim without a source. With citation choices turned off, the system picks the source for each claim. This run used automatic citation.

The dial sets which steps wait for a person. In the autonomous position, no step waits. In the second position, load-bearing citations and critical answers to referee findings wait for the person. In the third position, every answer waits. S10.text:
This work leaves three questions about impact open. We do not test whether papers that Galley produces go on to high citation impact. We also do not test whether Galley can produce such papers at high volume, or whether the seven-factor profile predicts impact. We state all three as open hypotheses.  

Methodological and evaluation scope are similarly bounded. The evidence here comes from one run on one seed, with one assignment of model families to seats and no baseline system; we do not test whether cross-family separation of duties catches more errors than single-family review, we do not evaluate the human-in-the-loop controls with users, and we do not check the generated package against any venue's submission requirements. We also do not compare the in-run checks against a pre-deployment offline test suite, so this work does not establish whether they catch the failures that an offline suite would detect. Separate model families may share failure modes, so one family's review need not catch another's errors. No person independently audited citation support, manuscript quality or the settlement of referee findings by fix, rebuttal, limitation or third-family adjudication. No person verified that the reconciled claim ledger, evidence package and sign-off sheet match the final text. Because the seed describes Galley itself, the seed's claims about how Galley works are the authors' own and rest on no external source, and the single run gives no independent test of the model-run review, data analysis or simulation behaviors. Only a model-run review reads full texts, with an independent model auditing each finding; outside one, Galley checks each citation against the cited work's abstract as found in OpenAlex. A work with no abstract there cannot supply a verified citation. A claim that rests on implementation choices, methods or results reported only in full text is either narrowed to what an abstract states or left as a hypothesis.

The seven-factor impact standard scores a seed before any text is written and scores the finished paper after review. Neither score is evidence of how the paper will be cited.

We do not test whether cross-family separation of duties catches more errors than single-family review. The rule is enforced in code, and the production record shows how it operated in the run. No experiment in this paper compares it with review in which one model family holds every seat on the same seeds. The paper therefore makes no claim about how well the rule detects errors relative to single-family review.

We do not evaluate the human controls with users. The paper describes the dial, threads, proposed changes, citation choices and the sign-off sheet as designed. The evaluated run used the autonomous dial, so no step waited for a person. The paper offers no evidence on whether people find these controls usable or whether using them changes the manuscript.

Outside a systematic review, Galley checks each citation against the cited work's abstract only. The verbatim match confirms that the supporting passage is copied from the abstract, and the verifier judges that passage against its claim. Neither step reads the full text. A verified citation therefore shows what the abstract states, not what the full text supports.

The evidence comes from one run on one seed, with one assignment of model families to seats and no baseline system. Every count in the production record describes that run alone. This includes the {{run.calibration}} planted defective citations that the verifier caught and the {{run.calibration_controls}} unaltered controls that it accepted. These counts do not estimate rates across seeds, fields or other assignments of families, and the paper does not compare Galley with any other system. S7.text:
In-run calibration is Galley's diagnostic audit of judgment reliability on a manuscript's own inputs. Unlike calibration in machine learning, no check adjusts model probabilities or decision thresholds. All three checks belong to improver behaviors rather than the seven skeleton behaviors (Section 4), and each runs when the paper's state makes its behavior ready on the ladder. First, during claim-level citation verification, code requires every proposed supporting passage to match the cited work's OpenAlex abstract verbatim (Section 5). Second, once a run has verified citations, the `calibrate` behavior tests the verifier on planted defects and verified controls. Third, after peer review finishes, a model family other than the author's reconciles the final text against every claim in the ledger through the `reconcile` behavior (Section 6). Verbatim matching rejects any proposed passage that does not match the abstract, and `reconcile` confirms, narrows or drops each ledger claim, whereas `calibrate` only measures: it reports two rates and, as an improver, cannot stop the paper from reaching `ready`. The production record reports which of these behaviors ran in the evaluated run, and Section 9 reports its citation-verification and calibration counts. As a design choice rather than a claim of equivalent test coverage, Galley relies on these in-run checks and keeps pre-deployment offline test suites minimal.

The `calibrate` behavior places deliberately defective citations (planted defects) alongside unaltered verified citations (controls), and the verifier judges the mixed set. A planted defect is defective by construction. Controls are drawn from this manuscript's verified citations. A control is a citation the verifier has already accepted during verification, so accepting it again shows consistency with that earlier judgment, not independently established accuracy. From these judgments `calibrate` measures two rates for this run's planted set alone, both reported in the production record: the proportion of planted defects the verifier catches and the proportion of unaltered controls it wrongly rejects. The `calibrate` implementation in Galley's source (https://github.com/autonomio/galley) defines how it selects controls, constructs planted defects and counts each of the verifier's three judgments, including narrower judgments, toward these rates. Pairing defects with controls prevents a trivial verifier that rejects every citation from appearing reliable, since such a verifier catches every planted defect while wrongly rejecting every control. The planted set is drawn from one manuscript's citations, and planted defects need not resemble the errors in naturally occurring candidates, so the rates do not estimate the verifier's accuracy beyond that set.

Galley checks the reliability of its own judgments inside each run, on the inputs of the manuscript at hand. We call this in-run calibration. It consists of three checks, marked A, B and C in Figure 3. The first is the verbatim match, which code enforces on every proposed citation. The second is planted-defect calibration, which the `calibrate` behavior performs on the verifier. The third is cross-family reconciliation, which the `reconcile` behavior performs on the final text. These checks take the place of long offline test suites run before deployment, so Galley keeps its offline tests minimal.

The case for checking inside the run rests on what the checks examine. An offline suite exercises a system on inputs fixed in advance. The judgments a manuscript depends on are made on its own claims, its own candidate passages and its own final text. In-run calibration examines those judgments on those inputs. The prompts and answers behind checks B and C are stored in the production journal with the rest of the run, and a rerun replays them without calling a model.

The verbatim match is the one check that no model performs. The checker proposes a passage from a candidate work's abstract in support of a claim. Code confirms that the passage is copied verbatim from that abstract, and no citation is accepted without this match. Separately, the verifier, a seat held by a family other than the checker's, judges whether the passage supports the claim, supports only a narrower claim, or does not support it. A passage that a model paraphrases or composes cannot pass the match, so it cannot stand behind a citation.

Planted-defect calibration tests the verifier itself. The `calibrate` behavior places planted defects, which are deliberately defective citations, among the verified citations. Alongside them it places controls, which are unaltered verified citations. The verifier then judges the mixed set. From these judgments `calibrate` measures two rates. The first is how many planted defects the verifier catches, which shows whether it rejects citations that should fail. The second is how many controls it wrongly rejects, which shows whether it rejects citations that should stand. Neither rate means much alone, because a verifier that rejected every citation would catch every planted defect and also reject every control. Like every improver, `calibrate` measures the paper but cannot stop it.

The production record reports both rates for the evaluated run. The verifier caught {{run.calibration}} planted defective citations and accepted {{run.calibration_controls}} unaltered controls. Both figures come from the production journal of that run. They describe the verifier's judgments on that manuscript's own citations.

Cross-family reconciliation checks the last stage of a claim's lifecycle. A referee answer marked as fixed comes with exact edits. Those edits change the text after its citations were verified, so the final manuscript can word a claim differently from the ledger entry that records it. Once review is done, `reconcile` gives a family other than the author's the final text to read against every claim in the claim ledger. That family confirms each claim, narrows it to the text's wording, or drops it as no longer stated. The ledger, the evidence package and the sign-off sheet then say what the manuscript says.

Together, the three checks follow a claim that needs external evidence from its first proposed citation to the final text, as Figure 3 shows. The verbatim match controls which passages can support a claim. Planted-defect calibration measures the verifier that accepts or rejects those passages. Reconciliation confirms that the final text still states what the ledger records. Each check acts on the manuscript's actual inputs. This is why Galley checks reliability during each run and does not depend on a test suite run once before release.

S11.text:
Six studies could build on cross-family separation of duties and in-run calibration. Study materials could include a production journal, a claim ledger and an evidence package.

The first is a controlled comparison of cross-family and single-family verification and review. For each judging behavior, such as citation verification or the judging of referee answers, the study would replay identical upstream steps from the journal and cross the producing family with the judging family across all nine pairings of three families, so no other seat enters the comparison. The study would report all nine cell means and estimate the average departure of the three same-family cells from what additive producer and judge effects predict; pairing-specific effects can also contribute to that contrast. Separating family matching from reuse of the identical model would require identical-model and distinct-model pairings within each family. Alongside in-run planted-defect, control and referee metrics, blinded human annotators would audit surviving claim–citation accuracy and manuscript quality.

The second would extend in-run calibration to full texts, analyses, simulations and figures. The study could pair planted defects with unaltered controls in full-text passages, numerical analysis outputs, simulation inputs and results, and compiled figures. The study would compare the verifier's performance on these materials with its performance on citation checks.

The third is a user study of the human controls. It would observe people using the dial, `@both` threads with their proposed changes, and the sign-off sheet. It would measure which decisions people take over and which proposed changes they accept. It would also measure whether the sign-off sheet directs their attention to the claims the system added and the claims stated as hypotheses.

The fourth is a prospective science-of-science test of the seven-factor profile. The study would score seeds and finished papers before publication and track citations to the papers afterward. The study would test whether the profile predicts subsequent citations.

The fifth is a seed-to-preprint benchmark. Participating systems would run the same seeds, and blinded assessors would use each output's claim ledger and evidence package to locate claims and source passages, judge support against a shared rubric, and report coverage of the seed's substantive claims alongside claims narrowed, dropped or left as hypotheses.

The sixth applies the pattern outside scholarly writing. We hypothesize that cross-family separation of duties transfers to clinical guidelines, legal briefs and intelligence assessments. The study could use at least three model families, assign claim writing and verification to different families, and record prompts and answers in a journal.

S9.text:
We evaluate Galley through one self-referential run. Galley produced this manuscript, which introduces Galley, from the authors' seed. The seed asked what sets very high-impact papers apart and presented Galley as a semi-autonomous, multi-agent editor built from atomic behaviors, each proven before the next is built. The run proposed three directions and selected one that recentres the paper on cross-family separation of duties and in-run calibration; the selecting family was not the family that proposed the directions. Galley ran with the dial set to autonomous, so no step waited for a person.   Every count and rate in this section comes from the production record, which Galley generates from the run's production journal. The journal stores every prompt and answer of the run in the paper's folder, and a rerun with Galley's source (https://github.com/autonomio/galley, MIT licence) replays them without calling a model, so each governed decision, such as the selection of a direction or the adjudication of a finding, is recorded as the stored answer of the seat that made it. Typesetting renders the claim ledger at the end of this manuscript from the surviving recorded claims, listing whether the seed or the system added each claim alongside its sources and reconciled standing. The run also writes an evidence package of claims, evidence and sources in the Resolvent format.

The run used automatic citation. The settings allowed 2 referee rounds, capped answers at 3, and allowed up to 10 candidate works per claim. 

    

The run took {{run.hours}} wall-clock hours from seed to this manuscript and made {{run.calls}} model calls. The run made {{run.calls_claude}} calls to Claude, {{run.calls_gpt}} to GPT and {{run.calls_gemini}} to Gemini. The run read {{run.tokens_in_m}} million input tokens and wrote {{run.tokens_out_k}} thousand output tokens. Galley ran {{run.behaviors}} behaviors.

The final argument contains {{run.claims}} claims. Of these, {{run.claims_seed}} came from the seed and the system added {{run.claims_added}}. Galley narrowed {{run.claims_narrowed}} claims. Of the claims marked as needing external evidence, {{run.claims_unsupported}} ended without verified evidence and are stated as hypotheses; claims marked as the authors' own work or as premises do not seek external citations. 

The evidence search screened {{run.works_screened}} candidate works. Galley verified {{run.citations_verified}} citations. It rejected {{run.citations_rejected}} proposed citations. During calibration, Galley detected {{run.calibration}} planted defects and accepted {{run.calibration_controls}} controls.

Over {{run.rounds}} referee rounds, the referee seats raised {{run.findings}} findings, and {{run.findings_material}} of them were material or critical. Galley resolved {{run.findings_resolved}} of the material or critical findings. Galley adjudicated {{run.findings_adjudicated}} findings.

 

In this paper, submission-ready means that Galley's own gates held on one revision of the manuscript. It does not mean that outside reviewers accepted the paper, and it does not replace the authors' review of the sign-off sheet. The evaluation reports governed decisions as counts; no single decision has been audited independently of the run's production journal. That sheet lists what only the authors can decide: declarations, the {{run.claims_added}} claims the system added, claims stated as hypotheses, decisions a third family made and skipped steps.

The final argument contains {{run.claims}} claims. Of these, {{run.claims_seed}} came from the seed and the system added {{run.claims_added}}. Galley narrowed {{run.claims_narrowed}} claims. Of the claims marked as needing external evidence, {{run.claims_unsupported}} ended without verified evidence and are stated as hypotheses; claims marked as the authors' own work or as premises do not seek external citations. 

The evidence search screened {{run.works_screened}} candidate works. Galley verified {{run.citations_verified}} citations. It rejected {{run.citations_rejected}} proposed citations. During calibration, Galley detected {{run.calibration}} planted defects and accepted {{run.calibration_controls}} controls.

Over {{run.rounds}} referee rounds, the referee seats raised {{run.findings}} findings, and {{run.findings_material}} of them were material or critical. Galley resolved {{run.findings_resolved}} of the material or critical findings. Galley adjudicated {{run.findings_adjudicated}} findings.

 

In this paper, submission-ready means that Galley's own gates held on one revision of the manuscript. It does not mean that outside reviewers accepted the paper, and it does not replace the authors' review of the sign-off sheet. The evaluation reports governed decisions as counts; no single decision has been audited independently of the run's production journal. That sheet lists what only the authors can decide: declarations, the {{run.claims_added}} claims the system added, claims stated as hypotheses, decisions a third family made and skipped steps.

figures.caption: Seats and the five decisions governed by cross-family separation of duties. Each decision is judged by a family other than the one that produced the work, and the rule is enforced in code, not in prompts.
figures.spec: Two panels side by side. Left panel: three rounded rectangles stacked vertically, one per model family, each a distinct color (family A blue, B orange, C green). Box A: 'Claude Opus 5.5 — author'. Box B: 'GPT-6.2 Sol — checker; referee seats (rotated between rounds)'. Box C: 'Gemini 4 Carbon — challenger; verifier; referee seats (rotated between rounds)'. Under each box, a small grey tag: 'own command-line client · no tools · no delegation · strict JSON answers'. Right panel: a table with five rows and four columns headed 'Decision', 'Work produced by', 'Judged by', 'Constraint checked in code'. Row 1: 'choose among reformulations' | 'family that proposed the three directions' | 'a different family' | 'judge ≠ proposer'. Row 2: 'accept a citation' | 'checker (GPT-6.2 Sol) proposes a verbatim abstract passage' | 'verifier (Gemini 4 Carbon)' | 'verifier ≠ checker'. Row 3: 'accept an answer to a referee finding' | 'author (Claude Opus 5.5)' | 'the referee seat that raised the finding (GPT-6.2 Sol or Gemini 4 Carbon)' | 'referee ≠ author'. Row 4: 'settle a finding disputed after 3 answers' | 'author and referee in dispute' | 'adjudicator: the remaining family' | 'adjudicator ∉ {author, referee}'. Row 5: 'reconcile final text with claim ledger' | 'author (Claude Opus 5.5)' | 'a family other than the author's' | 'reconciler ≠ author'. Where a cell names a specific family, fill it lightly in that family's color; cells naming 'a different family' or 'the remaining family' are hatched grey. Thin arrows run from each family box on the left to the cells it occupies. A full-width band beneath both panels reads 'production journal: every prompt and answer stored in the paper folder; a rerun replays them without calling a model'. No numbers other than those shown.

figures.caption: The ladder of 27 atomic behaviors in scan order. Solid boxes are the seven skeleton behaviors that make a paper exist; dashed boxes are improvers that make it better but cannot stop it. The scheduler scans from behavior 1, runs whatever is ready and rescans from 1 after any behavior settles.
figures.spec: Three columns of nine boxes, read top to bottom, then left to right, numbered 1–27. Column 1: 1 extract, 2 position, 3 review-idea, 4 reformulate, 5 select-direction, 6 literature-review, 7 analyze, 8 simulate, 9 plan. Column 2: 10 outline, 11 find-evidence, 12 verify, 13 reassess, 14 calibrate, 15 draft, 16 figure, 17 fidelity, 18 frame. Column 3: 19 referee, 20 close-round, 21 respond, 22 verify-disposition, 23 adjudicate, 24 reconcile, 25 reprofile, 26 typeset, 27 ready. Each box shows its group as a small text tag and a fill color from a seven-color legend: skeleton (1, 9, 10, 15, 26), aim (2–5), substance (6, 8, 16), truth (7, 11–14, 17), manuscript (18), referees (19–23), close (24, 25, 27). Boxes 1, 9, 10, 15, 18, 26 and 27 have a thick solid border and the label 'required'; the other 20 boxes have a dashed border and the label 'improver'. Boxes 6, 7 and 8 carry an extra tag 'only when the authors request it or supply data'. At the top, an arrow labeled 'text seed (only required input)' enters a cylinder labeled 'paper state (paper folder)' drawn to the right of the columns; one double-headed arrow per column connects the column to the cylinder, labeled 'read state / write result'. Along the left margin, a looping arrow labeled 'scheduler: scan from 1 → run what is ready → after any behavior settles, rescan from 1'. At the bottom, an output tray listing 'PDF · line-numbered review PDF · LaTeX · Word · editor document · evidence package (Resolvent format) · sign-off sheet · production journal'. Legend in the lower right.

#set page(width: 16cm, height: auto, margin: 6pt)
#set text(font: "New Computer Modern", size: 9pt)
#set par(leading: 0.5em, justify: false)

#let accent = rgb("#2b5797")
#let fills = (
  skeleton: accent.lighten(62%),
  aim: luma(252),
  substance: luma(224),
  truth: accent.lighten(88%),
  manuscript: accent.lighten(76%),
  referees: luma(200),
  close: luma(242),
)
#let req-stroke = 1.6pt + luma(10)
#let imp-stroke = (paint: luma(55), thickness: 0.8pt, dash: (3pt, 2pt))

// geometry
#let bw = 3.65cm
#let colx = (1.25cm, 5.15cm, 9.05cm)
#let yT = 2.85cm
#let gap = 0.16cm
#let hn = 0.88cm
#let ht = 1.45cm
#let h2 = 1.07cm
#let yB = yT + 6 * hn + 3 * ht + 8 * gap
#let cx0 = 13.05cm
#let cw = 2.4cm
#let eh = 0.4cm
#let ct = 0.8cm
#let cb = 4.9cm
#let lanes = (1.3cm, 1.85cm, 2.4cm)
#let H = 15.85cm

// (number, name, group, required, conditional)
#let ladder = (
  (1, "extract", "skeleton", true, false),
  (2, "position", "aim", false, false),
  (3, "review-idea", "aim", false, false),
  (4, "reformulate", "aim", false, false),
  (5, "select-direction", "aim", false, false),
  (6, "literature-review", "substance", false, true),
  (7, "analyze", "truth", false, true),
  (8, "simulate", "substance", false, true),
  (9, "plan", "skeleton", true, false),
  (10, "outline", "skeleton", true, false),
  (11, "find-evidence", "truth", false, false),
  (12, "verify", "truth", false, false),
  (13, "reassess", "truth", false, false),
  (14, "calibrate", "truth", false, false),
  (15, "draft", "skeleton", true, false),
  (16, "figure", "substance", false, false),
  (17, "fidelity", "truth", false, false),
  (18, "frame", "manuscript", true, false),
  (19, "referee", "referees", false, false),
  (20, "close-round", "referees", false, false),
  (21, "respond", "referees", false, false),
  (22, "verify-disposition", "referees", false, false),
  (23, "adjudicate", "referees", false, false),
  (24, "reconcile", "close", false, false),
  (25, "reprofile", "close", false, false),
  (26, "typeset", "skeleton", true, false),
  (27, "ready", "close", true, false),
)

#let beh(n, name, group, req, cond, hh) = {
  let rows = (
    text(9pt, box(width: 12pt, text(fill: accent, strong(str(n)))) + strong(name)),
    text(8pt, fill: luma(35), [#group] + h(1fr) + (if req { strong("required") } else { [improver] })),
  )
  if cond {
    rows.push(text(8pt, style: "italic", fill: luma(30))[only when the authors request it or supply data])
  }
  rect(
    width: bw, height: hh, radius: 2pt, inset: (x: 4pt, y: 3pt),
    fill: fills.at(group),
    stroke: if req { req-stroke } else { imp-stroke },
    align(horizon + left, stack(dir: ttb, spacing: 3pt, ..rows)),
  )
}

#let ah(x, y, dir, col: luma(50)) = {
  let l = 0.2cm
  let w = 0.075cm
  let pts = if dir == "down" {
    ((x, y), (x - w, y - l), (x + w, y - l))
  } else if dir == "up" {
    ((x, y), (x - w, y + l), (x + w, y + l))
  } else if dir == "right" {
    ((x, y), (x - l, y - w), (x - l, y + w))
  } else {
    ((x, y), (x + l, y - w), (x + l, y + w))
  }
  place(top + left, polygon(fill: col, stroke: none, ..pts))
}

#let seg(a, b, s) = place(top + left, line(start: a, end: b, stroke: s))

#let sw(f, s) = box(width: 0.5cm, height: 0.32cm, fill: f, stroke: s, radius: 1.5pt, baseline: 0.1cm)

#let legend-entry(key, nums) = (
  sw(fills.at(key), 0.5pt + luma(90)),
  [#key \ #text(fill: luma(70))[#nums]],
)

#let legend = block(width: 2.5cm, {
  set text(8pt)
  set par(leading: 0.4em, spacing: 5pt)
  set block(spacing: 5pt)
  text(9pt, strong[fill: group])
  grid(
    columns: (0.6cm, 1fr), row-gutter: 6pt,
    ..legend-entry("skeleton", "1, 9, 10, 15, 26"),
    ..legend-entry("aim", "2–5"),
    ..legend-entry("substance", "6, 8, 16"),
    ..legend-entry("truth", "7, 11–14, 17"),
    ..legend-entry("manuscript", "18"),
    ..legend-entry("referees", "19–23"),
    ..legend-entry("close", "24, 25, 27"),
  )
  v(4pt)
  text(9pt, strong[border])
  grid(
    columns: (0.6cm, 1fr), row-gutter: 6pt,
    sw(white, req-stroke), [*required* \ makes a paper exist],
    sw(white, imp-stroke), [improver \ makes it better, cannot stop it],
  )
})

#block(width: 15.5cm, height: H, {
  // ---- the ladder: three columns of nine behaviors ----
  for c in range(3) {
    let y = yT
    for k in range(9) {
      let (n, name, group, req, cond) = ladder.at(c * 9 + k)
      let hh = if c == 0 { if cond { ht } else { hn } } else { h2 }
      place(top + left, dx: colx.at(c), dy: y, beh(n, name, group, req, cond, hh))
      y += hh + gap
    }
  }

  // ---- paper state cylinder ----
  let cstroke = 0.9pt + luma(30)
  place(top + left, dx: cx0, dy: cb - eh / 2, ellipse(width: cw, height: eh, fill: luma(242), stroke: cstroke))
  place(top + left, dx: cx0, dy: ct, rect(width: cw, height: cb - ct, fill: luma(242), stroke: (left: cstroke, right: cstroke, top: none, bottom: none)))
  place(top + left, dx: cx0, dy: ct - eh / 2, ellipse(width: cw, height: eh, fill: luma(226), stroke: cstroke))
  place(top + left, dx: cx0 + 0.1cm, dy: 1.25cm, block(width: cw - 0.2cm, {
    set align(center)
    set par(leading: 0.42em, spacing: 4pt)
    text(9pt)[*paper state* \ (paper folder)]
    v(3pt)
    text(8pt, fill: luma(30))[every prompt and answer is stored here; a rerun replays them without calling a model]
  }))

  // ---- text seed entering the cylinder ----
  let sx = cx0 + cw / 2
  seg((sx, 0.02cm), (sx, ct - eh / 2 - 0.2cm), (paint: accent, thickness: 1.1pt))
  ah(sx, ct - eh / 2, "down", col: accent)
  place(top + left, dx: sx - 5.2cm, dy: 0.08cm, box(width: 5cm, align(right, text(9pt)[*text seed* (only required input)])))

  // ---- one double-headed arrow per column: read state / write result ----
  let lane-stroke = (paint: luma(50), thickness: 0.8pt, cap: "square")
  for c in range(3) {
    let rx = colx.at(c) + 0.45cm
    let ly = lanes.at(c)
    seg((rx, ly), (rx, yT - 0.2cm), lane-stroke)
    seg((rx, ly), (cx0 - 0.2cm, ly), lane-stroke)
    ah(rx, yT, "down")
    ah(cx0, ly, "right")
    place(top + left, dx: rx + 0.15cm, dy: ly - 0.33cm, text(8pt, fill: luma(35))[read state / write result])
  }

  // ---- scheduler loop along the left margin ----
  let loop-stroke = (paint: accent, thickness: 1.1pt, cap: "square")
  let lx = 0.95cm
  let by = yB + 0.34cm
  let b1y = yT + hn / 2
  let c3x = colx.at(2) + bw / 2
  seg((c3x, yB), (c3x, by), loop-stroke)
  seg((c3x, by), (lx, by), loop-stroke)
  seg((lx, by), (lx, b1y), loop-stroke)
  seg((lx, b1y), (colx.at(0) - 0.2cm, b1y), loop-stroke)
  ah(colx.at(0), b1y, "right", col: accent)
  place(top + left, dx: 0.04cm, dy: (b1y + by) / 2 - 5.25cm,
    rotate(-90deg, reflow: true, block(width: 10.5cm, {
      set align(center)
      set par(leading: 0.5em)
      text(8.5pt)[#text(fill: accent)[*scheduler:*] scan from 1 → run what is ready → \ after any behavior settles, rescan from 1]
    })))

  // ---- output tray ----
  let tx0 = colx.at(0)
  let tx1 = colx.at(2) + bw
  let ty0 = 14.45cm
  let ty1 = 15.8cm
  place(top + left, polygon(fill: luma(246), stroke: none, (tx0, ty0), (tx1, ty0), (tx1 - 0.2cm, ty1), (tx0 + 0.2cm, ty1)))
  let tray-stroke = (paint: luma(35), thickness: 1.1pt, cap: "round")
  seg((tx0, ty0), (tx0 + 0.2cm, ty1), tray-stroke)
  seg((tx0 + 0.2cm, ty1), (tx1 - 0.2cm, ty1), tray-stroke)
  seg((tx1 - 0.2cm, ty1), (tx1, ty0), tray-stroke)
  place(top + left, dx: tx0 + 0.35cm, dy: ty0 + 0.3cm, block(width: tx1 - tx0 - 0.7cm, {
    set par(leading: 0.55em)
    text(9pt)[*output:* PDF · #box[line-numbered review PDF] · LaTeX · Word · #box[editor document] · #box[evidence package (Resolvent format)] · #box[sign-off sheet] · #box[production journal]]
  }))

  // ---- legend, lower right ----
  place(bottom + right, legend)
})

figures.caption: Lifecycle of a claim that needs external evidence, with the three in-run checks marked A (verbatim match, enforced by code), B (planted-defect calibration) and C (cross-family reconciliation). No rates are drawn; the production record reports them for the run.
figures.spec: Left-to-right flowchart; rectangles are states or behaviors, diamonds are decisions, and the three in-run checks use one accent color with circled labels A, B, C. (1) Rectangle 'claim in plan — kind: needs external evidence'. (2) Rectangle 'find-evidence: searches via Canary over OpenAlex; up to 10 candidate works per claim'. (3) Rectangle 'checker (GPT-6.2 Sol) proposes a passage from a candidate abstract'. (4) Diamond A 'code: passage copied verbatim from the abstract?' — 'no' arrow returns to (3) labeled 'next candidate'; 'yes' arrow continues. (5) Diamond 'verify (Gemini 4 Carbon)' with three exits: 'supported' → rectangle 'verified citation'; 'narrower' → rectangle 'claim narrowed to the passage' → 'verified citation'; 'not supported' → back to (3) labeled 'citation rejected; next candidate'. A small note on 'verified citation': 'work with a DOI: bibliographic record from the DOI registry'. From (3), a dashed arrow labeled 'candidates exhausted' leads down to rectangle 'stated as hypothesis', then to diamond 'reassess (if load-bearing): thesis stands / narrows / fails'. (6) Below the verified-citation path, accent-colored panel B 'calibrate': a row of tokens mixing verified citations (plain), planted defective citations (marked ✗) and unaltered controls (marked ○), with an arrow into 'verifier' and two output labels 'share of defects caught' and 'share of controls wrongly rejected' → small box 'production record'. (7) Main path continues: 'draft' → 'fidelity' → 'referee rounds (2 in this run)'. (8) Accent-colored diamond C 'reconcile (family other than the author's)' with three exits 'confirmed', 'narrowed to the text's wording', 'dropped as no longer stated', all converging on (9) a stacked box 'claim ledger · evidence package (Resolvent) · sign-off sheet'.
figures.source:
#set page(width: 16cm, height: auto, margin: 6pt)
#set text(font: "New Computer Modern", size: 9pt)
#set par(leading: 0.5em, justify: false)

#let u = 1cm
#let ink = luma(35)
#let accent = rgb("#2b5797")
#let tint = accent.lighten(86%)
#let tint2 = accent.lighten(93%)

// straight segment; all coordinates in cm from the canvas top-left
#let seg(x1, y1, x2, y2, paint: ink, th: 0.6pt, dash: none) = place(top + left,
  line(start: (x1 * u, y1 * u), end: (x2 * u, y2 * u),
    stroke: (paint: paint, thickness: th, dash: dash,
      cap: if dash == none { "square" } else { "butt" })))

// polyline with an arrowhead at the last point
#let arr(..pts, paint: ink, th: 0.6pt, dash: none, hs: 0.17) = {
  let p = pts.pos()
  let n = p.len()
  let (ax, ay) = p.at(n - 2)
  let (bx, by) = p.at(n - 1)
  let dx = bx - ax
  let dy = by - ay
  let l = calc.sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy)
  let ux = dx / l
  let uy = dy / l
  let w = hs * 0.42
  for i in range(n - 2) {
    let (x1, y1) = p.at(i)
    let (x2, y2) = p.at(i + 1)
    seg(x1, y1, x2, y2, paint: paint, th: th, dash: dash)
  }
  seg(ax, ay, bx - ux * hs * 0.8, by - uy * hs * 0.8, paint: paint, th: th, dash: dash)
  place(top + left, polygon(fill: paint, stroke: none,
    (bx * u, by * u),
    ((bx - hs * ux + w * uy) * u, (by - hs * uy - w * ux) * u),
    ((bx - hs * ux - w * uy) * u, (by - hs * uy + w * ux) * u)))
}

#let node(x, y, w, h, body, fill: white, stroke: 0.6pt + ink, radius: 2pt, inset: 3pt) = place(
  top + left, dx: x * u, dy: y * u,
  rect(width: w * u, height: h * u, fill: fill, stroke: stroke, radius: radius, inset: inset,
    align(center + horizon, body)))

#let dia(cx, cy, w, h, body, fill: white, stroke: 0.6pt + ink) = {
  place(top + left, polygon(fill: fill, stroke: stroke,
    ((cx - w / 2) * u, cy * u), (cx * u, (cy - h / 2) * u),
    ((cx + w / 2) * u, cy * u), (cx * u, (cy + h / 2) * u)))
  place(top + left, dx: (cx - w / 2) * u, dy: (cy - h / 2) * u,
    block(width: w * u, height: h * u, align(center + horizon, body)))
}

#let lab(x, y, w, h, body, al: center + horizon, it: true) = place(
  top + left, dx: x * u, dy: y * u,
  block(width: w * u, height: h * u,
    align(al, if it { text(style: "italic", body) } else { body })))

#let mark(cx, cy, l, r: 0.22) = {
  place(top + left, dx: (cx - r) * u, dy: (cy - r) * u,
    circle(radius: r * u, fill: accent, stroke: none))
  place(top + left, dx: (cx - r) * u, dy: (cy - r) * u,
    block(width: 2 * r * u, height: 2 * r * u,
      align(center + horizon, text(fill: white, weight: "bold", size: 8pt, l))))
}

#let chip(x, y, kind, s: 0.36) = {
  node(x, y, s, s, [], fill: luma(238), stroke: 0.5pt + luma(110), radius: 1.2pt, inset: 0pt)
  if kind == "x" {
    let m = s * 0.24
    seg(x + m, y + m, x + s - m, y + s - m, th: 0.9pt)
    seg(x + s - m, y + m, x + m, y + s - m, th: 0.9pt)
  } else if kind == "o" {
    let r = s * 0.25
    place(top + left, dx: (x + s / 2 - r) * u, dy: (y + s / 2 - r) * u,
      circle(radius: r * u, fill: none, stroke: 0.8pt + ink))
  }
}

#block(width: 15.5cm, height: 13.55cm, {
  set text(size: 8pt)

  // ---------- notation key ----------
  node(0, 0.13, 0.5, 0.32, [], radius: 1pt)
  lab(0.62, 0.07, 2.6, 0.44, al: left + horizon, it: false)[state or behavior]
  dia(3.6, 0.29, 0.56, 0.36, [])
  lab(4.0, 0.07, 1.6, 0.44, al: left + horizon, it: false)[decision]
  node(0, 0.7, 0.5, 0.32, [], fill: tint, stroke: 0.9pt + accent, radius: 1pt)
  lab(0.62, 0.64, 4.0, 0.44, al: left + horizon, it: false)[in-run check (A, B, C)]

  // ---------- row 1: claim to verbatim check ----------
  node(0, 1.75, 2.5, 1.9)[*claim in plan* \ kind: needs external evidence]
  node(3.0, 1.75, 3.5, 1.9)[*find-evidence* \ searches via Canary over OpenAlex; up to 10 candidate works per claim]
  node(7.05, 1.75, 3.25, 1.9)[*checker* (GPT-6.2 Sol) proposes a passage from a candidate abstract]
  dia(12.95, 2.7, 4.2, 2.4, fill: tint, stroke: 1pt + accent)[*code:* passage \ copied verbatim \ from the abstract?]
  mark(11.2, 1.75, "A")
  arr((2.5, 2.7), (3.0, 2.7))
  arr((6.5, 2.7), (7.05, 2.7))
  arr((10.3, 2.7), (10.85, 2.7))

  // A: no -> back to checker
  arr((12.95, 1.5), (12.95, 1.15), (9.7, 1.15), (9.7, 1.75))
  lab(9.75, 0.67, 3.15, 0.44)[no: next candidate]

  // verify: not supported -> back to checker
  arr((14.95, 5.5), (15.35, 5.5), (15.35, 0.5), (7.9, 0.5), (7.9, 1.75))
  lab(8.0, 0.02, 7.3, 0.44)[not supported: citation rejected; next candidate]

  // A: yes -> verify
  arr((12.95, 3.9), (12.95, 4.5))
  lab(13.05, 3.93, 0.9, 0.5, al: left + horizon)[yes]
  dia(12.95, 5.5, 4.0, 2.0)[*verify* \ (Gemini 4 Carbon)]

  // narrower
  node(7.55, 5.05, 2.2, 0.9)[claim narrowed to the passage]
  arr((10.95, 5.5), (9.75, 5.5))
  lab(9.75, 5.06, 1.2, 0.4)[narrower]
  arr((8.65, 5.95), (8.65, 6.6), (11.6, 6.6), (11.6, 6.95))

  // supported
  arr((12.95, 6.5), (12.95, 6.95))
  lab(13.05, 6.5, 1.6, 0.45, al: left + horizon)[supported]
  node(11.05, 6.95, 3.8, 1.65)[*verified citation* \ #text(style: "italic")[work with a DOI: bibliographic record from the DOI registry]]

  // candidates exhausted -> hypothesis -> reassess
  arr((7.3, 3.65), (7.3, 4.9), (6.85, 4.9), dash: (3pt, 2pt))
  lab(7.4, 3.73, 3.0, 0.45, al: left + horizon)[candidates exhausted]
  node(4.4, 4.45, 2.45, 0.9)[stated as hypothesis]
  arr((4.4, 4.9), (3.8, 4.9))
  dia(2.0, 4.9, 3.6, 1.8)[*reassess* \ (if load-bearing)]
  arr((2.0, 5.8), (2.0, 6.1))
  lab(0, 6.1, 4.0, 0.42, it: false)[thesis stands / narrows / fails]

  // ---------- panel B: calibrate ----------
  node(0, 7.0, 10.4, 3.25, [], fill: tint2, stroke: 0.9pt + accent, radius: 3pt)

adjudication.decision: narrow: Both sides are partly right. The author is right that relying on in-run checks while keeping pre-deployment offline test suites minimal is an explicit design choice from the seed (C22) and part of the thesis, so framing it strictly as a design choice rather than cutting all mention of it preserves an actual property of the system without claiming measured equivalence. The referee is right that (1) no evidence compares the in-run checks against an offline test suite, so S1 and S7 must frame the relationship strictly as a design choice rather than an established functional replacement and S10 must record the missing comparison once as a limitation of the work; and (2) all three checks belong to improver behaviors rather than the seven skeleton behaviors, so the Abstract, S1, and S7 must not state that every run exercises them and instead must specify the conditions under which each check runs (claim-level citation verification for verbatim abstract matching, verified citations for planted-defect calibration, and completed peer review for closing reconciliation), scoping empirical demonstration to the evaluated run.

edits.new: In-run calibration audits a manuscript's inputs through behaviors that enforce verbatim abstract matching during claim-level citation verification, test the verifier with planted defects once citations are verified, and reconcile the final text across model families after peer review.
edits.old: In-run calibration checks reliability on each manuscript's own inputs through code-enforced verbatim matching against abstracts, planted defective citations, and cross-family reconciliation of the final text.

edits.new: Our thesis is that a semi-autonomous scholarly editor can turn a raw text seed into a submission-ready preprint across isolated, replayable atomic behaviors, under a code-enforced rule that no model family judges its own output and with in-run checks auditing reliability on the manuscript's inputs. As a design choice, Galley relies on these in-run checks and keeps pre-deployment offline test suites minimal. Galley's unattended run producing this manuscript demonstrates this workflow on one seed.
edits.old: Our thesis is that a semi-autonomous scholarly editor can be run from a raw text seed to a submission-ready preprint across isolated, replayable atomic behaviors, under a code-enforced rule that no model family judges its own output, with its reliability checked inside each run rather than by offline test suites, as Galley's own unattended run producing this manuscript shows.

edits.new: - **In-run calibration**: diagnostic checks on a manuscript's own inputs that Galley uses as a design choice instead of extensive pre-deployment offline test suites. During claim-level citation verification, code checks that each proposed passage appears verbatim in the cited work's abstract. Once a run has verified citations, the calibrate behavior plants defective citations alongside unaltered controls and measures how many defects the verifier catches and how many controls it wrongly rejects. After peer review finishes, a family other than the author's reconciles the final text against every claim in the ledger.
edits.old: - **In-run calibration**: checks on each manuscript's own run in place of offline test suites. Code confirms that every cited passage is copied verbatim from the cited work's abstract, the calibrate behavior plants defective citations and unaltered controls among the verified ones and measures how many the verifier catches, and a family other than the author's reconciles the final text against every claim in the ledger.

edits.new: In-run calibration is Galley's diagnostic audit of judgment reliability on a manuscript's own inputs. Unlike calibration in machine learning, no check adjusts model probabilities or decision thresholds. All three checks belong to improver behaviors rather than the seven skeleton behaviors (Section 4), and each runs when the paper's state makes its behavior ready on the ladder. First, during claim-level citation verification, code requires every proposed supporting passage to match the cited work's OpenAlex abstract verbatim (Section 5). Second, once a run has verified citations, the `calibrate` behavior tests the verifier on planted defects and verified controls. Third, after peer review finishes, a model family other than the author's reconciles the final text against every claim in the ledger through the `reconcile` behavior (Section 6). The evaluated run exercised all three checks (Section 9). As a design choice rather than a claim of equivalent test coverage, Galley relies on these in-run checks and keeps pre-deployment offline test suites minimal.
edits.old: Galley checks the reliability of its own judgments inside a run, on the inputs of the manuscript at hand. We call this in-run calibration. It is a per-run diagnostic audit, not calibration in the machine-learning sense: no check adjusts model probabilities or decision thresholds. It consists of three checks. The first is the verbatim match, which code enforces on every passage proposed as citation evidence. The second is planted-defect calibration, which the `calibrate` behavior performs on the verifier. The third is cross-family reconciliation, which a different model family performs on the final text. Galley uses these checks instead of long offline test suites run before deployment and keeps its offline tests minimal. This substitution is a design choice, not a measured equivalence: the checks have not been shown to detect every failure that such a suite would detect.

edits.new: The evidence here comes from one run on one seed, with one assignment of model families to seats and no baseline system; we do not test whether cross-family separation of duties catches more errors than single-family review, and we do not evaluate the human-in-the-loop controls with users. We also do not compare the in-run checks against a pre-deployment offline test suite, so this work does not establish whether they catch the failures that an offline suite would detect.

dispositions.text: S5 states the rubric's origin: it is the authors' own design heuristic, not one taken from prior work, and S10 leaves its predictive validity open. S5 also gives the procedure. The screen scores each of seven factors, names the weakest and returns one of three verdicts: worth writing, reformulate or no contribution. A verdict can redirect the paper but cannot stop it. The paper's thesis and load-bearing claims concern cross-family separation of duties, verbatim-gated citation and in-run calibration. None of them depends on the factor names or on a score-to-verdict threshold, and the paper does not use the rubric as evidence of impact. The system definition this paper reports refers to seven factors but does not name them or give a numeric decision rule. Adding either would describe system behaviour with no basis in that definition, so S5 should not be changed.

verification.reason: S5 identifies the rubric as the authors' design heuristic and lists its possible verdicts. It omits the seven factor names, their scoring rules and the rule that maps scores to verdicts.

adjudication.decision: adopt_author: Rounds 1 and 2 resolved the attribution and validity issues raised by the citations referee. S5 identifies the seven-factor rubric as the authors' own design heuristic rather than an external standard, states its input-to-verdict procedure as a non-blocking improver (worth writing, reformulate, or no contribution), and S10 leaves predictive validity open as an untested hypothesis. Neither the thesis, any load-bearing claim, nor any result reported in S9 depends on the individual factor names, factor-level scoring criteria, or score-to-verdict mapping rule; the governed cross-family decision in S5 is direction selection after a reformulate verdict, and other non-load-bearing improvers such as reassess and fidelity are specified at the same input-to-verdict level. Moreover, the seed, claim ledger, and production record in the request do not specify the seven factor names, scoring criteria, or verdict mapping rule. Supplying them would invent details absent from the record, whereas stating in the prose that the manuscript omits them would comment on what the text documents rather than state a limitation of the work itself.

Our thesis is that a semi-autonomous scholarly editor can turn a text seed into a submission-ready preprint package across isolated, replayable atomic behaviors under a code-enforced rule that no model family evaluates its own work and with reliability checked inside each run, as Galley's unattended run producing this manuscript shows; whether papers produced this way achieve high citation impact remains an open hypothesis.

The paper makes three contributions:

- **Cross-family separation of duties**: a reusable governance pattern, enforced in code across at least three model families with a prompt-and-answer journal, ensuring no family selects among its own reformulations, verifies its own citations, judges its own referee responses, adjudicates its own disputes or reconciles its own final manuscript.

- **Galley and its provenance package**: an open-source 27-behavior semi-autonomous scholarly editor with optional human controls that produces submission-ready manuscript files alongside a claim ledger, evidence package, sign-off sheet and replayable production journal.
