edit.new:
A second gap separates a valuable idea from a paper ready to submit. Agent pipelines can draft text, but LLM-generated scholarly text can contain misattributed citations [@lai2026hallucinatio; @linardon2026fluency], and LLMs used as evaluators tend to rate their own outputs more favorably than outputs from other models [@panickssery2024llm; @chen2025beyond].

Galley is a semi-autonomous, multi-agent scholarly editor organized around a ladder of 27 isolated, replayable atomic behaviors. From a text seed, it produces a submission-ready preprint package containing the manuscript as a PDF, a line-numbered review PDF, LaTeX and Word, together with its claim ledger, Resolvent evidence package, sign-off sheet and production journal. To address evaluator self-preference and citation error, Galley enforces cross-family separation of duties in code so that no model family selects among its own reformulations, verifies its own citations, judges its own referee responses, adjudicates its own disputes or reconciles its own final manuscript, paired with in-run calibration on each manuscript's actual inputs.

Our thesis is that a semi-autonomous scholarly editor can produce a submission-ready preprint package from a text seed across replayable atomic behaviors governed by code-enforced cross-family separation of duties and in-run calibration, as shown by an autonomous run that produced this manuscript. Whether papers produced this way achieve high citation impact remains open.

The paper makes the following contributions:

- **Cross-family separation of duties and in-run calibration**: a reusable governance pattern requiring at least three model families and a prompt-and-answer journal, combining code-enforced cross-family review across five decisions with per-run verbatim abstract matching, planted-defect calibration and closing reconciliation.
- **A 27-behavior semi-autonomous scholarly editor**: Galley, an open-source system with optional human-in-the-loop controls that turns a text seed into submission and review files (PDF, line-numbered review PDF, LaTeX and Word) alongside a claim ledger, evidence package, sign-off sheet and replayable production journal.
- **Self-referential end-to-end evaluation**: an autonomous three-family run that produced this manuscript from a text seed, audited through its own production journal, claim ledger and planted-defect calibration.

## Multi-agent systems for scholarly production

Agent systems already automate parts of scholarly production, including writing scientific surveys and checking that citations support the claims they are attached to [@yang2026deepsurvey]. DeepSurvey is a direct example. It extracts structured keynotes and models relationships across papers through clustering and comparative analysis. It also recovers implementation-level details with a code-agent subsystem. For reliability, it combines citation-graph expansion with hybrid filtering for topic-focused retrieval and constrains analysis and writing to evidence. It uses agentic refinement at several levels to check citation–claim alignment [@yang2026deepsurvey].

Galley shares DeepSurvey's concern with citation reliability. DeepSurvey generates surveys. Galley turns a seed, the text a person supplies, into a pre-publication academic manuscript.

edit.new:
## The ladder and the scheduler

The ladder is the ordered list of the 27 atomic behaviors: (1) `extract`, (2) `position`, (3) `review-idea`, (4) `reformulate`, (5) `select-direction`, (6) `literature-review`, (7) `analyze`, (8) `simulate`, (9) `plan`, (10) `outline`, (11) `find-evidence`, (12) `verify`, (13) `reassess`, (14) `calibrate`, (15) `draft`, (16) `figure`, (17) `fidelity`, (18) `frame`, (19) `referee`, (20) `close-round`, (21) `respond`, (22) `verify-disposition`, (23) `adjudicate`, (24) `reconcile`, (25) `reprofile`, (26) `typeset` and (27) `ready`.

The scheduler scans the ladder from the top, runs whatever is ready from the paper's current state, and scans again from the top whenever any behavior settles. Readiness decides whether a behavior can run, and position on the ladder decides which ready behavior a scan reaches first. After a behavior settles, the next scan can run a newly ready behavior higher on the ladder—for example, `find-evidence` (11) and `verify` (12) when `respond` (21) requests new evidence—so no behavior needs to know that it must loop.

## Skeleton behaviors and improvers

Minor issues do not block work. Only the seven skeleton behaviors are required for a paper to exist: `extract` (1), `plan` (9), `outline` (10), `draft` (15), `frame` (18), `typeset` (26) and `ready` (27). The remaining twenty behaviors are improvers that can strengthen the paper without being able to stop it, so small defects do not halt production.

edit.new: Whereas Sections 5 and 6 detail code-enforced verbatim abstract matching and cross-family closing reconciliation, planted-defect calibration tests the verifier itself. The `calibrate` behavior places deliberately defective citations (planted defects) alongside unaltered verified citations (controls), and the verifier judges the mixed set. From these judgments `calibrate` measures two rates, both reported in the production record: the proportion of planted defects the verifier catches and the proportion of unaltered controls it wrongly rejects. Pairing defects with controls prevents a trivial verifier that rejects every citation from appearing reliable, since such a verifier catches every planted defect while wrongly rejecting every control.

Planted-defect calibration tests the verifier itself. The `calibrate` behavior places planted defects, which are deliberately defective citations, among the verified citations. Alongside them it places controls, which are unaltered verified citations. The verifier then judges the mixed set. From these judgments `calibrate` measures two rates. The first is the proportion of planted defects the verifier catches. The second is the proportion of unaltered controls the verifier wrongly rejects. A verifier that rejects every citation catches every planted defect and wrongly rejects every control.

The production record reports both rates for the evaluated run. They describe the verifier's judgments on the planted defects and unaltered controls.

Cross-family reconciliation checks how the final text states the claims. A different model family performs this check.

The three checks address proposed citation passages, verifier judgments and the final text. The verbatim match limits citation evidence to passages that appear verbatim in the cited abstracts. Planted-defect calibration measures how the verifier judges the mixed set of citations. Reconciliation checks the claims in the final text. Each check acts on the manuscript's actual inputs.

dispositions.text:
The ledger the referee is reading cannot be the final ledger. The fix the referee asks for would also break the rule this paper argues for.

(1) Order of steps. Referee, close-round, respond, verify-disposition and adjudicate (ladder steps 19–23) must all finish before reconcile (step 24) can run. Any manuscript a referee reads therefore carries the ledger from before reconciliation. C40, C29 and C48 are the two kinds of entry reconcile settles after review. C40 is a claim recorded more strongly than the text now states it, and C29 and C48 are claims the text no longer makes. S6 already states this order and says the gaps are what reconciliation takes as input.

(2) Who may change the entries. If the author corrected or dropped C40, C29 and C48, the author's family would be judging its own claims. The code-enforced rule forbids this. A family other than the author's makes that change.

(3) The nine narrowed claims in S9. The production record the referee read was generated from the journal before reconcile ran, so none of those nine is a reconciliation outcome. They record narrowings made before review ended. Reconcile writes each claim's outcome to the journal at step 24. The production record of the submitted manuscript is generated from that journal. The material available to this section does not include those counts, and the section does not invent them.

(4) Companion artifacts. S6 states that typeset renders the manuscript with its ledger, the evidence package and the sign-off sheet from the same revision. It also states that ready (step 27) passes only when every gate holds on one revision. The three agree because all are rendered from that one revision, not because they are compared afterwards. Whether a review packet includes the evidence package and the sign-off sheet is a question about the packet, not about the system.

adjudication.decision: narrow: Both sides are partly right. The author is right on execution order, separation of duties and available data: reconcile (step 24) runs only after referee review, responses, judgments and adjudication (steps 19–23) settle; Appendix A is generated from the claim ledger at typesetting rather than edited directly; the author family cannot edit ledger standings without judging its own claims; companion artifacts are derived from the same state at typesetting rather than compared separately; and post-reconciliation counts cannot be invented before step 24 runs. However, the referee is right that the manuscript prose currently overclaims what reconciliation and the self-referential evaluation establish: Sections 6 and 8 assert unconditionally that after reconciliation the ledger, evidence package and sign-off sheet say what the manuscript says, even though reconciliation is an uncalibrated, unaudited model judgment on recorded claims; Abstract and Section 9 attribute pre-reconciliation ledger counts (45 claims, 27 system-added claims, 5 unsupported claims stated as hypotheses) to the reconciled final argument and report 9 narrowed claims without identifying that those narrowings occurred during citation verification; and Section 10 omits closing reconciliation and companion artifacts from its list of unaudited outputs. The edits narrow Sections 6, 8, 9, 10 and the Abstract to that common ground.

edits.old: A gap separates a valuable idea from a paper ready to submit. Agent systems automate parts of scholarly production, but text generated by large language models (LLMs) can contain misattributed citations, and LLM evaluators tend to favor their own outputs. This paper presents Galley, an open-source, semi-autonomous, multi-agent scholarly editor. Through a ladder of 27 atomic behaviors, it turns a text seed into a preprint package that is submission-ready under Galley's own gates rather than any venue's requirements, with a claim ledger, evidence package, sign-off sheet and replayable production journal. dispositions.text:
Two separate mechanisms produce agreement, and S6 states both.

First, reconciliation makes the ledger agree with the text. A family other than the author's reads the final text against every recorded claim and confirms, narrows or drops each one. This happens at step 24, after referee review (steps 19–23) is over. The entries the referee cites (C40, C29, C48) are in the ledger from before reconciliation, which is the only ledger a referee can see. They are the cases reconciliation exists to settle. If the author rewrote them, the author's family would be judging its own claims, which the code-enforced rule forbids. Asking the author to make the change would weaken the paper's thesis rather than repair the text.

Second, rendering keeps the three artifacts in agreement. Typeset renders the manuscript with its ledger, the evidence package and the sign-off sheet from the same revision. Ready marks the paper ready only once every gate holds on one revision. Because all three come from one state, no later comparison is needed to make them agree. Whether referees receive the evidence package and sign-off sheet is a question about the review packet, not about how the work behaves.

The referee's third request, limiting the guarantee to recorded claims, is already in S6. The earlier answers' edits remain in place, and no further edit can change what a ledger from before reconciliation contains.

adjudication.decision: narrow: Both seats are partly right. The author is right that in Galley's 27-step ladder, reconciliation runs at step 24 after peer review and adjudication (steps 19-23) finish, code forbids the author's family from reconciling its own claims, and Appendix A is generated from the claim ledger at typesetting rather than edited directly; pre-reconciliation discrepancies such as C40, C29 and C48 and the unavailability of reconciled companion files during review follow from that order. The referee is right that Sections 6 and 8 still state post-reconciliation agreement with the manuscript prose as an unconditional guarantee, conflate single-revision derivation of claim entries across the three rendered outputs with prose-to-ledger verification, and omit from the evaluation limitations that alignment of the reconciled artifacts with the final text went unverified. The edits narrow Sections 6 and 8 so claim-to-text alignment on recorded claims rests explicitly on the reconciling family's judgment while single-revision typesetting aligns claim entries across the appended ledger, evidence package and sign-off sheet after review ends, and state once in Section 10 that no person verified that those reconciled artifacts match the final text.

edits.new:
Closing reconciliation checks the claim ledger against the post-review text. Once peer review finishes, a family other than the author's reads the final text against every claim in the claim ledger and assigns each claim one of three outcomes. It confirms a claim that the text still states as recorded. It narrows a claim to the text's wording when the text now says less than the ledger. It drops a claim that the text no longer states. The production journal stores each outcome with the claim it applies to. Because reconciliation follows peer review and adjudication, referees read the pre-reconciliation ledger, and the typeset step renders the reconciled ledger, evidence package and sign-off sheet only after review ends.

Reconciliation aligns recorded claims with the text through a cross-family model judgment, and the typeset step propagates the resulting ledger across the companion artifacts. Reconciliation works from the recorded claims and updates the ledger rather than the text, so an assertion that never entered the ledger lies outside its check. The reconciling family's judgment decides which recorded claims remain in the ledger and how the ledger states them. Claims that reconciliation drops do not appear in the appended ledger, the evidence package or the sign-off sheet. When the text or ledger changes, the typeset step renders the manuscript with its appended ledger, the evidence package and the sign-off sheet from the same revision. Those three outputs therefore carry the same claim entries by derivation from one revision rather than by a comparison after rendering. The ready step marks the paper ready for submission only once every gate holds on one revision. Code enforces the cross-family seat assignment for reconciliation, while claim-to-text agreement on recorded claims rests on that family's judgment rather than a code check.

Section 2 notes that extending model-level self-preference to whole developer families is a design precaution, Appendix A shows 25 of 40 claims are "the authors' own work," and Section 9 reports 20 of 27 behaviors ran (with no systematic review, dataset analysis, or simulation).
findings.decision: Add to Section 10's methodological limitations that (1) no independent human audit evaluated citation support, manuscript quality, or resolved referee findings (which include accepted rebuttals, limitation statements, and third-family adjudications alongside fixes), (2) separate model families can share correlated failure modes while intra-family bias itself is untested here, and (3) this self-referential run chiefly evaluates system-design claims typed as the authors' own work without exercising systematic review, local data analysis, or simulation.

The single run also gives no independent test of the systematic review, data analysis or simulation behaviors. findings.evidence: Section 3 ("Seat assignment in this run") states that Claude Opus 5.5 held the author seat, GPT-6.2 Sol held the checker seat, Gemini 4 Carbon held both the challenger and verifier seats, and "Each referee was either GPT-6.2 Sol or Gemini 4 Carbon." Deductively, with three families, excluding the author's family forces the citations referee and reconciler to come from the exact same families that earlier proposed (`checker`), verified (`verifier`), or framed (`challenger`) the manuscript's citations and direction.
findings.decision: Clarify in Section 3 that with the minimum of three model families, separation holds per governed decision relative to that step's producer rather than across all earlier seats in the run, so non-author referee seats (including the citations referee) and reconciliation necessarily reuse the families that held `checker`, `verifier`, and `challenger` roles earlier in the pipeline.

findings.alternatives: Either a closing step extracts all factual assertions from the final prose and checks both directions between prose and ledger (which no behavior on the 27-step ladder performs), or closing reconciliation guarantees alignment only for claims recorded in the ledger without detecting unrecorded prose assertions or rewriting post-review overstatements.
findings.evidence: Section 6 states that during closing reconciliation a family other than the author's "reads the final text against every claim in the claim ledger and assigns each claim one of three outcomes" (`confirm`, `narrow` when the text says less than the ledger, or `drop` when no longer stated), and Section 8 already narrows its ledger description to "For each claim the run records." findings.decision: Scope Section 6's reconciliation guarantee to claims recorded in the ledger and state explicitly that because `reconcile` starts from recorded ledger entries and updates only the ledger, it does not detect prose assertions that never entered the ledger or rewrite sentences strengthened during review or human editing.

findings.quote: Large language models serving as judges tend to favor their own responses over those generated by other models [@chen2025beyond], so a model family that reviews its own draft does not provide an independent check.
findings.question: Does `[@chen2025beyond]` establish that any model within a developer's model family is biased toward another model in that family, or only that an individual model favors its own responses—making family-level separation a design precaution rather than a deduced fact?
findings.alternatives: Either `@chen2025beyond` empirically demonstrates cross-model bias across distinct models within the same developer's model family (which its verified passage does not), or `@chen2025beyond` establishes only model-level self-preference and extending separation to an entire developer family is Galley's design precaution, as Section 2 states.
findings.evidence: The verified passage for `[@chen2025beyond]` states: "Recent studies show that large language models (LLMs) exhibit self-preference bias when serving as judges, meaning they tend to favor their own responses over those generated by other models." Section 2 ("Self-preference in LLM evaluators") explicitly notes that "Both works describe the preference of an individual model for its own outputs" and that "Family-level separation is a design precaution motivated by this model-level evidence," contradicting Section 1's deductive "so a model family that reviews its own draft does not provide an independent check."
findings.decision: Revise Section 1's second paragraph so `@chen2025beyond` supports non-independence when the same model drafts and reviews, and frame the extension to the developer's entire model family as a design precaution consistent with Section 2.

edit.new: Large language models serving as judges tend to favor their own responses over those generated by other models [@chen2025beyond], so assigning drafting and review to the same model does not provide an independent check; as a design precaution, Galley extends this separation to the developer's entire model family.
edit.old: Large language models serving as judges tend to favor their own responses over those generated by other models [@chen2025beyond], so a model family that reviews its own draft does not provide an independent check.

The edit given under F2-citations-2 limits the non-independence conclusion to a model that reviews its own draft. It states the family-level separation as a design precaution, consistent with Section 2.

verification.reason: Section 1 restricts the non-independence conclusion from [@chen2025beyond] to a model reviewing its own draft and frames extending separation to the developer's model family as a design precaution consistent with Section 2.

findings.quote: The study would cross the family that produces each output with the family that judges it, across all nine pairings of three families, and hold every other seat at one fixed assignment.
findings.question: In a three-family pool, how can an end-to-end study cross the producing and judging families across all nine pairings while holding every other seat (such as `adjudicator` and `reconciler`) at one fixed assignment without causing same-family collisions in off-diagonal cells and violating Galley's adjudication rule?
findings.alternatives: Either Study 1 tests each producer–judge decision in isolation on shared upstream inputs (or draws its fixed seats from additional families outside the three crossed families) and estimates the mean diagonal departure from additive main effects, or holding other seats fixed from a three-family pool creates same-family collisions across off-diagonal cells.
findings.evidence: Section 3 establishes that adjudication requires a third family distinct from both the author's and the referee's (`adjudicator != author` and `adjudicator != referee`) and reconciliation requires `reconciler != author`. In a three-family pool $\{F_1, F_2, F_3\}$, varying `(producer, judge)` over all nine pairings while holding `adjudicator` or `reconciler` at one fixed family from $\{F_1, F_2, F_3\}$ forces that "fixed" seat to match the producer or judge in subsets of the six off-diagonal cells, violating third-family adjudication and confounding cross-family cells. Moreover, in a $3 \times 3$ table (4 interaction degrees of freedom), only the mean diagonal departure (1 df) is identified separately from off-diagonal pair interactions without further restrictions.
findings.decision: Specify in Section 11 that the $3 \times 3$ crossing either isolates each governed decision on shared upstream inputs or holds remaining seats fixed using families outside the three crossed ones, and define the family-matching estimator as the mean departure of the three same-family cells from additive producer and judge main effects.

edit.new: For each governed decision tested on shared upstream inputs (or in full runs whose remaining seats are held fixed using families outside the three crossed ones), the study would cross the producing family with the judging family across all nine pairings of three families. The average effect of family matching is the mean departure of the three same-family cells from what additive main effects of the producing and judging families predict, removing each family's main output and judging effects.
edit.old: The study would cross the family that produces each output with the family that judges it, across all nine pairings of three families, and hold every other seat at one fixed assignment. The effect of family matching is how far the three same-family cells depart from what the main effects of the producing and judging families predict, so neither the quality of a family's output nor the ability of a judging family enters the estimate.

dispositions.text: Correct. With only three families, holding the adjudicator or reconciler at one fixed family would collide with a crossed family in some off-diagonal cells. The revision takes the first option the referee offers. Each judging behavior is tested alone on identical upstream steps replayed from the journal. Galley stores every prompt and answer, and a rerun replays them without calling a model, so only the producing and judging families vary and no other seat enters the comparison. The estimator the referee asked for (the mean departure of the three same-family cells from additive producer and judge effects) is in the edit given under F2-editor-10.

edits.old: The study would cross the family that produces each output with the family that judges it, across all nine pairings of three families, and hold every other seat at one fixed assignment.
edits.new: For each judging behavior, such as citation verification or the judging of referee answers, the study would replay identical upstream steps from the journal and cross the producing family with the judging family across all nine pairings of three families, so no other seat enters the comparison.

verification.reason: Section 11 resolves the three-family seat-collision issue by isolating each judging behavior on identical upstream steps replayed from the journal across all nine producer-by-judge family pairings so no other seat enters the comparison, and defines the estimator as the average departure of the three same-family cells from additive producer and judge effects.

findings.quote: Each family runs through its own command-line client with no tools and answers in a strict JSON schema, and every prompt and answer is stored, so a rerun replays the run without calling a model.
findings.question: Does storing model prompts and answers let a rerun replay "the run" in full—including external OpenAlex retrieval, DOI registry calls, local data analysis, simulations, and typesetting—or only the recorded model exchanges?
