F1-methods-2 (What evidence establishes that these checks cover the failures an offline test suite would address, or that every run exercises all three checks?) was settled by gemini: narrow. Both sides are partly right. The author is right that relying on in-run checks while keeping pre-deployment offline test suites minimal is an explicit design choice from the seed (C22) and part of the thesis, so framing it strictly as a design choice rather than cutting all mention of it preserves an actual property of the system without claiming measured equivalence. The referee is right that (1) no evidence compares the in-run checks against an offline test suite, so S1 and S7 must frame the relationship strictly as a design choice rather than an established functional replacement and S10 must record the missing comparison once as a limitation of the work; and (2) all three checks belong to improver behaviors rather than the seven skeleton behaviors, so the Abstract, S1, and S7 must not state that every run exercises them and instead must specify the conditions under which each check runs (claim-level citation verification for verbatim abstract matching, verified citations for planted-defect calibration, and completed peer review for closing reconciliation), scoping empirical demonstration to the evaluated run.

F1-methods-3 (Which artifacts did the run produce, which readiness gates passed on the same revision, and did anyone check the package against the intended venue's requirements?) was settled by gemini: narrow. Both the author and the referee are partly right. The referee is right that the abstract still uses 'submission-ready' at first use without qualifying it as readiness under Galley's own gates rather than a venue's requirements, and that S1's wording ('marks the paper ready only once every gate holds on one revision') states completion broadly without reflecting how bounded that check is. The author is right that S1 already lists the final-revision deliverables and qualifies readiness at first use in the introduction, and that the source material and claim ledger do not specify named individual sub-gates inside the ready behavior or per-gate pass results, which are unknown from the provided material and cannot be invented. The edits narrow the text to the common ground: they qualify 'submission-ready' at first use in the abstract, narrow S1 to state that only seven of the 27 behaviors are required, that ready checks only that Galley's internal gates hold on one revision (not venue rules or external review), and that the production record reports what each behavior did, and state in Limitations (S10) that the evaluation does not check the generated package against any venue's submission requirements.

F1-methods-1 (The methods section presents configured referee rounds as completed rounds. What parts of cross-family review did the run actually exercise?) was settled by gemini: narrow. Both seats are partly right. The author is right that Section 6 already states the two-round limit as a configured bound, that Appendix A is generated from the claim ledger at typesetting rather than edited directly in manuscript text (closing reconciliation narrows C11 to the manuscript wording after review), and that copying Section 9's counts into Section 6 as fixed numbers could contradict Section 9 when typesetting regenerates those counts from the production journal. The referee is right that Section 6 pointed only to the production record and omitted Section 9, which reports the run's counts inside the manuscript, without stating the conditions under which between-round seat rotation and adjudication execute, and that the manuscript did not bound its empirical evaluation claims to the behaviors and review steps actually executed in the run. Two edits narrow the text to the common ground: Section 6 states the configured two-round bound and the preconditions for seat rotation and adjudication while citing both Section 9 and the production record for completed counts, and Section 10 limits the evaluation in Limitations to the subset of the 27 atomic behaviors and the referee rounds and adjudications executed in the autonomous run.

F1-methods-4 (Which closest systems were inspected for family assignment and enforcement, and what establishes the claimed difference?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. Section 3 already removes the categorical comparison with prior systems and limits code-enforced cross-family separation of duties to the five governed decisions, as the referee acknowledges. No other prose section states the removed comparison, and evidence search for C48 found no supporting passage. Appendix A renders the claim ledger at typesetting and does not take direct prose edits during review responses or adjudication. Closing reconciliation runs after adjudication and narrows C40 to match the wording in Section 3. Because the manuscript text already meets the referee's substantive requirements, the author's last answer stands with no edits.

F1-methods-9 (What are the seven factors and the scoring rules that turn their ratings into a reformulation verdict?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. S5 already frames the seven-factor standard as the authors' unvalidated design heuristic, clarifies that as an improver the screen can redirect a paper toward reformulation rather than stop it, and includes the original idea alongside the three proposed directions in cross-family selection. The remaining items requested by the referee—the names of the seven factors, their scoring scale, and any rule mapping factor scores to a verdict—are not known from the material in this request, so adding them would invent system behavior. No claim in the thesis and no metric reported in S9 depends on the factor names or on a score threshold; the argument relies only on the rule that a family other than the proposing family selects among the original idea and the three proposed directions, while S10 already states as a limitation that the seven-factor profile has not been tested as a predictor of citation impact. The author's last answer therefore stands with no edits.

F1-methods-8 (Which evidence route is subject to the abstract-only gate?) was settled by gemini: narrow. Both seats are partly right. Section 5 already scopes the verbatim abstract gate to claim-level evidence search and describes how a systematic review searches OpenAlex, reads full texts, quotes passages and audits each finding with an independent model, though its second verification paragraph leaves 'each such citation' ambiguous immediately after the sentence on systematic reviews. Claim C34 in Appendix A is generated from the claim ledger rather than edited directly in manuscript prose, and closing reconciliation narrows ledger claims against the final text. The referee is right, however, that Section 7 (and the summary of in-run calibration in Section 1) still states the verbatim check across every cited or proposed passage without limiting it to claim-level evidence search. The edits clarify the antecedent in Section 5 and narrow the statements in Sections 1 and 7 to claim-level evidence search so that the manuscript is internally consistent and closing reconciliation narrows C34 accordingly.

F1-citations-1 (Which prior systems lack an enforced rule separating the producing and judging model families?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. The author's final response resolves the finding in the manuscript text. Both the author and the referee agree that Section 3 drops the novelty comparison against prior systems, and verification against OpenAlex abstracts found no verbatim passage showing how DeepSurvey, SciSage, DeepReviewer 2.0 or DeepSciVerify assign producing and judging model families. No section of the manuscript states C48 or claims which prior systems lack cross-family separation of duties. The referee objects only that C40 and C48 remain in Appendix A, which typesetting generates from the claim ledger rather than from direct text edits. Under the behavior order in Section 4 and Section 6, closing reconciliation runs after review and adjudication finish, narrows C40 to what the text states, and drops C48 because the manuscript does not state it.

F1-citations-2 (Did the evaluated run exercise the referee loop?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. The author's last answer stands because S6 already satisfies the requested manuscript changes and Galley updates the claim ledger at closing reconciliation rather than through direct edits to Appendix A. Across all three rounds, the referee confirms that S6 separates configured settings from completed activity and presents answer judgment and adjudication as implemented mechanisms. S6 states only the configured cap of three answers per finding and the configured limit of two referee rounds, while S9 reports the run counts from the production record. The referee's remaining objection concerns C11 in Appendix A, which still states that the run used two referee rounds. Galley generates Appendix A from the claim ledger at typesetting and does not accept direct text edits to that appendix. Under the ladder in S4 and the closing check in S6, the reconcile behavior runs after peer review under a family other than the author's and narrows C11 to match the revised text before the typeset behavior regenerates Appendix A. Finally, although the referee disputes a remark in the author's rebuttal about whether a round formally closed, S6 makes no claim that a round closed.

F1-methods-5 (How were defects and controls selected, how were their expected labels established, and how did a narrower judgment count?) was settled by gemini: narrow. Both sides are partly right. What is not known from the material in this request is how calibrate selects controls from the verified citations, how it constructs planted defects, and how it scores narrower judgments toward the two calibration rates; stating those rules in prose would invent facts, while Section 7 already limits both rates to this run's planted set and distinguishes control consistency from independently established accuracy, and Section 9 and the Abstract report the case counts (6 of 6 planted defects and 2 of 2 controls). At the same time, the referee is right that Section 7 overreaches by stating that every control was already judged supported, because Section 5 and Claim C34 allow verified citations to be accepted under either supported or narrower judgments, and Section 7's reference to calibrate in Galley's source omitted control selection and the verifier's three-way judgment, including narrower judgments, while leaving Galley's uncapitalized. The edits narrow Section 7 to state that controls were accepted during verification and that calibrate in Galley's source defines control selection, planted-defect construction, and how all three verifier judgments, including narrower judgments, count toward the two rates.

F1-citations-8 (What are the seven factors, and where did the rubric come from?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. Rounds 1 and 2 resolved the attribution and validity issues raised by the citations referee. S5 identifies the seven-factor rubric as the authors' own design heuristic rather than an external standard, states its input-to-verdict procedure as a non-blocking improver (worth writing, reformulate, or no contribution), and S10 leaves predictive validity open as an untested hypothesis. Neither the thesis, any load-bearing claim, nor any result reported in S9 depends on the individual factor names, factor-level scoring criteria, or score-to-verdict mapping rule; the governed cross-family decision in S5 is direction selection after a reformulate verdict, and other non-load-bearing improvers such as reassess and fidelity are specified at the same input-to-verdict level. Moreover, the seed, claim ledger, and production record in the request do not specify the seven factor names, scoring criteria, or verdict mapping rule. Supplying them would invent details absent from the record, whereas stating in the prose that the manuscript omits them would comment on what the text documents rather than state a limitation of the work itself.

F1-citations-5 (Which citation pathway is subject to the abstract-only gate?) was settled by gemini: adopt_referee. The referee is right that the manuscript still states the verbatim abstract gate without scope outside S5. S5 distinguishes claim-level abstract matching from systematic-review full-text auditing, whereas the abstract, S1 and S7 still describe verbatim abstract matching without restricting it to citations from claim-level evidence search, and S5's second verification paragraph leaves 'each such citation' immediately after the sentence on systematic reviews. The edits restrict the verbatim abstract gate to citations from claim-level evidence search across the abstract, S1, S5 and S7. Appendix A (including C34) is generated from the claim ledger rather than edited directly, and closing reconciliation aligns C34 with the scoped manuscript text.

F1-citations-9 (Where can a reader inspect the literature index and the retrieval component used by Galley?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. Section 5 already cites OpenAlex [@priem2022openalex; @priem2024openalex] where it first names the index and identifies Galley's MIT-licensed repository at https://github.com/autonomio/galley as containing Galley's source, including its calls to Canary. The material in this request gives no separate URL, repository, license or citation for Canary's own retrieval and systematic-review implementation, so the location of Canary's own code is not known from the record. Adopting the referee's demand would invent a source location, stating that Canary is unreleased would invent an unsupported fact about the software, and noting that the manuscript omits a Canary link would comment on what the text documents rather than state a limitation of the work itself. Section 5 does not claim that the Galley repository contains Canary's implementation, and accepted citations can be checked against their cited works through the passages and sources recorded in the claim ledger and the Resolvent evidence package. The author's last answer stands with no edits.

F2-field-1 (Why does the claim ledger retain a load-bearing novelty claim that the manuscript withdrew for lack of evidence?) was settled by gemini: adopt_author. The author's rebuttal stands because the manuscript body already excludes the disputed claims and the claim ledger updates only during post-review reconciliation. Neither the title, the abstract nor Sections 1–11 state C40's comparison with the closest prior systems or the unverified hypotheses in C29, C46 and C48, as the referee acknowledges in Round 3. Typesetting generates Appendix A from the claim ledger rather than from direct text edits, so manuscript edits cannot alter those ledger entries. Under the behavior ladder in Section 4 and the reconciliation design in Section 6, reconcile (behavior 24) and typeset (behavior 26) run after referee, respond, verify-disposition and adjudicate (behaviors 19–23) finish. During review and adjudication, Appendix A therefore shows the pre-reconciliation ledger, and its gaps against the reviewed body text provide the input that reconcile corrects once review closes. Cross-family separation of duties in Section 3 assigns ledger reconciliation to a model family other than the author's after review ends, and Section 9 states the finished manuscript's properties rather than narrating an intermediate production stage.

F2-field-2 (What establishes agreement across the final artifacts when the supplied ledger contradicts the manuscript on recorded claims?) was settled by gemini: narrow. Both seats are partly right. The author is right that in Galley's 27-step ladder, reconciliation runs at step 24 after peer review and adjudication (steps 19-23) finish, code forbids the author's family from reconciling its own claims, and Appendix A is generated from the claim ledger at typesetting rather than edited directly; pre-reconciliation discrepancies such as C40, C29 and C48 and the unavailability of reconciled companion files during review follow from that order. The referee is right that Sections 6 and 8 still state post-reconciliation agreement with the manuscript prose as an unconditional guarantee, conflate single-revision derivation of claim entries across the three rendered outputs with prose-to-ledger verification, and omit from the evaluation limitations that alignment of the reconciled artifacts with the final text went unverified. The edits narrow Sections 6 and 8 so claim-to-text alignment on recorded claims rests explicitly on the reconciling family's judgment while single-revision typesetting aligns claim entries across the appended ledger, evidence package and sign-off sheet after review ends, and state once in Section 10 that no person verified that those reconciled artifacts match the final text.

F2-field-7 (What makes the automated workflow a systematic review whose search, screening, and findings another team could audit?) was settled by gemini: adopt_referee. The referee is right that the documented workflow supports finding-level verification against quoted full-text passages and an independent model audit rather than an auditable systematic review, and that the manuscript must use one term consistently. Section 5 already defines the workflow as a "model-run review" and states its finding-level audit grain, whereas Sections 3 and 10 still retain "systematic review". Replacing "systematic review" with "model-run review" in Section 3 (with a cross-reference to Section 5) and in both occurrences in Section 10 unifies the term across all editable manuscript sections, from which closing reconciliation updates ledger claims C7 and C42 (Appendix A is generated from the claim ledger and is not edited directly).

F2-editor-1 (How can this run demonstrate reconciliation when its published ledger still contains claims that contradict or exceed the final text?) was settled by gemini: narrow. Both sides are partly right. The author is right on execution order, separation of duties and available data: reconcile (step 24) runs only after referee review, responses, judgments and adjudication (steps 19–23) settle; Appendix A is generated from the claim ledger at typesetting rather than edited directly; the author family cannot edit ledger standings without judging its own claims; companion artifacts are derived from the same state at typesetting rather than compared separately; and post-reconciliation counts cannot be invented before step 24 runs. However, the referee is right that the manuscript prose currently overclaims what reconciliation and the self-referential evaluation establish: Sections 6 and 8 assert unconditionally that after reconciliation the ledger, evidence package and sign-off sheet say what the manuscript says, even though reconciliation is an uncalibrated, unaudited model judgment on recorded claims; Abstract and Section 9 attribute pre-reconciliation ledger counts (45 claims, 27 system-added claims, 5 unsupported claims stated as hypotheses) to the reconciled final argument and report 9 narrowed claims without identifying that those narrowings occurred during citation verification; and Section 10 omits closing reconciliation and companion artifacts from its list of unaudited outputs. The edits narrow Sections 6, 8, 9, 10 and the Abstract to that common ground.

Final profile: input_not_output 2/3, shared_bottleneck 2/3, conventional_body_one_graft 2/3, surprising_and_certain 0/3, opens_more_than_closes 2/3, cheap_to_adopt 2/3, early 2/3. Weakest: surprising_and_certain. Compared with the pre-drafting seed (2, 1, 1, 0, 2, 1, 2), the finished manuscript raises shared_bottleneck, conventional_body_one_graft, and cheap_to_adopt from 1 to 2 by recentring on citation fabrication and evaluator self-preference, grounding Related Work in 23 verified OpenAlex citations across five literature streams, and extracting a standalone three-family governance pattern alongside an MIT-licensed codebase. However, surprising_and_certain remains at 0—and under a multiplicative standard where one near-zero factor sinks a paper, the manuscript should be reformulated rather than sent out as-is. To stay faithful to its evidence, the run narrowed its thesis to a tautological internal existence claim ('submission-ready under its own gates' on one self-referential seed with no baseline and no human audit), where 26 of 44 ledger claims needed no external evidence as the authors' own work or premises, 4 of 18 external claims (including the core gap claim C29) ended as unverified hypotheses, and calibration checked only 6 planted defects and 2 previously accepted controls. Reframing the paper around the controlled 3x3 cross-family versus single-family replay experiment proposed in Section 11—evaluated on external seeds with blinded human audits while trimming residual science-of-science and system-tour sprawl—is needed to convert an honest architectural demonstration into a surprising, certain empirical contribution.

brief.concern: The author wants to know what actually sets very high-impact papers apart, and wants anyone with a valuable idea to be able to turn it into a strong, submission-ready paper without tooling friction, endless checks or manual work getting in the way.
brief.contribution: Galley is a semi-autonomous, multi-agent editor that runs several model families. It turns a text seed into a submission-ready pre-publication manuscript through a chain of atomic behaviors that are each proven before the next is built, with agent review loops, change proposals the human controls, and human-visible provenance.
brief.field: Human-computer interaction (AI-assisted scholarly writing and multi-agent LLM systems)
brief.audience: Researchers and builders of AI-assisted writing and multi-agent LLM tools, science-of-science researchers interested in what drives paper impact, research software engineers, and academics who want to turn ideas into submission-ready manuscripts

factors.name: input_not_output
factors.evidence: Galley (@autonomio/galley 0.1.0, MIT licence) is an open-source software capability that emits structured epistemic artifacts—a reconciled claim ledger, a human sign-off sheet, a Resolvent evidence package, and a replayable prompt-and-answer journal—rather than a closed finding about one run. However, the seed frames the paper around internal autonomio ecosystem couplings (poise in C3–C4 and C18, canary in C7–C8, and an unsettled resolvent design question in C10), scope notes (C5), software-testing opinions (C22–C23), and an unanswered impact question (C1), while requiring multi-vendor CLI clients (Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.2 Sol, Gemini 4 Carbon) that not all readers already own.
factors.improve: Strip internal roadmap and testing commentary (C5, C10, C22–C23) and unsubstantiated impact promises (C9, C21), and elevate Galley's transferable primitives—the monotonic skeleton-versus-improver protocol, reconciled claim-ledger/sign-off specification, and planted-defect verifier calibration harness—into a portable standard or benchmark others can run on any model setup.

factors.name: shared_bottleneck
factors.evidence: The number of researchers blocked from reaching submission is unknown, and the supplied queries (6,926 works on manuscript-preparation workload, 33 works dated 2026 across queries, and a 2023 study of submission guidelines across 302 leading biomedical journals, W4376131615) provide journal and publication counts rather than an author headcount. Moreover, the seed conflates two different problems: trustworthy, low-friction manuscript preparation and claim verification (an active concern in the literature alongside biomedical submission compliance) versus turning text seeds into high-impact papers at thousands-of-papers volume (C9, C21), which does not match documented author bottlenecks.
factors.improve: Anchor the bottleneck strictly in the documented trustworthiness and compliance gap of AI-assisted manuscript preparation—verifying claim-citation alignment, preserving traceable provenance, and maintaining human accountability—and quantify author friction directly via empirical workload data or systematic synthesis rather than assuming researchers are blocked by a lack of high-volume seed-to-paper generation.

factors.name: conventional_body_one_graft
factors.evidence: Within HCI (AI-assisted scholarly writing and multi-agent LLM systems), the idea connects to prior work on provenance (HaLLMark), automated survey generation (SciSage, DeepSurvey), claim-citation verification (DeepSciVerify), and auditable review (DeepReviewer 2.0), and contains a promising graft from software engineering and institutional design (poise's atomic state-machine ladder paired with cross-family separation of duties). Yet the seed breaks HCI conventions by claiming human-controlled proposed changes and collaborative threads (C12–C15) while planning a zero-human evaluation (C26; dial autonomous), asserting anti-testing polemics (C22–C23), and stacking multiple unrelated grafts at once, including an unanswered science-of-science theory of impact (C1–C2) and mass paper production (C21).
factors.improve: Write the body entirely in HCI and scholarly-verification language—grounded in mixed-initiative provenance and claim-verification benchmarks, without anti-testing claims (C22–C23) or mass-impact promises (C9, C21)—and retain one sharp graft: institutional separation of powers across distinct model families with fault-injected calibration over a monotonic atomic ladder.

factors.name: surprising_and_certain
factors.evidence: Against all three parts of the standard—improbable beforehand, undeniable afterwards, and holding up in strangers' hands—the seed as stated fails. Automated multi-agent drafting, peer review, and claim-citation verification are partly anticipated by 2025–2026 systems (SciSage, DeepSurvey, DeepReviewer 2.0, DeepSciVerify), so generating one preprint is not surprising beforehand. Headline claims of producing papers with projected high-impact potential from a seed alone (C9) at thousands-of-papers volume (C21) are unproven because C1 leaves what drives impact unanswered and whether the seven-factor profile predicts citation impact remains unknown. Human-control claims (C12–C15) go completely untested under autonomous settings and C26's no-manual-intervention rule, while C22–C23 reject extensive testing despite C24 claiming each behavior is proven. Although the underlying system enforces verbatim abstract checks, runs planted-defect verifier calibration (calibrate), reconciles a claim ledger, and logs a replayable journal, C26 tests N=1 self-referential preprint from the authors' own seed with zero strangers, zero external domains, and zero baseline comparisons.
factors.improve: Reframe the thesis immediately around verifiable epistemic governance rather than unproven high-impact prediction (stating C1/C9 strictly as open hypotheses and scoping C12–C15 as architectural mechanisms rather than user-tested outcomes), backed by hard internal measurements from calibrate (planted-defect catch and false-alarm rates), cross-family review/adjudication records, ledger reconciliation, and analytical or simulated error-propagation bounds; to reach 3, evaluate across diverse external seeds in strangers' hands against SciSage, DeepSurvey, DeepSciVerify, and single-family baselines, plus a human study of the interactive review controls.

factors.name: opens_more_than_closes
factors.evidence: Beneath the seed's monolithic tool pitch lie fertile follow-up questions for multi-agent systems, HCI, and science of science: whether cross-family role separation measurably cuts correlated hallucinations and review sycophancy versus single-family ensembles, how to extend live planted-defect calibration (calibrate) from OpenAlex abstracts to full texts and computed results, whether authors rubber-stamp or critically audit human sign-off sheets and @both change proposals across dial settings, and whether pre-writing structural profiles predict citation outcomes after controlling for network position and positive-result bias. Currently, presenting Galley as a finished engine for mass high-impact output obscures these research openings.
factors.improve: Frame each architectural mechanism—cross-family non-self-review, in-flight verifier calibration, monotonic skeleton-versus-improver scheduling, and reconciled sign-off ledgers—as a testable design hypothesis with explicit diagnostic metrics and stated boundaries (such as abstract-only verification outside systematic reviews), making follow-on experiments obvious to builders, HCI researchers, and scientometricians.

factors.name: cheap_to_adopt
factors.evidence: Although @autonomio/galley 0.1.0 is MIT-licensed on GitHub, the seed violates 'a noun the field needs, one idea, and something usable outside its original setting.' Claims C1–C26 bundle at least six competing ideas (bias-free impact profiling, poise atomic behaviors, multi-family adjudication, mixed-initiative diff/comment UI, canary and resolvent tooling, and minimal-testing philosophy) without coining one clear noun, and running the full tool requires separate CLI clients across multiple model families plus external search infrastructure.
factors.improve: Distill one memorable noun for one portable idea—such as cross-family epistemic governance or in-flight verifier calibration with reconciled claim ledgers—decoupled from poise/canary/resolvent branding and multi-CLI setup friction, so builders of legal, clinical, intelligence, or scientific synthesis systems can adopt the pattern directly.

factors.name: early
factors.evidence: Generic LLM writing provenance (HaLLMark, 2024) and single-slice multi-agent survey generation, review, and claim checking (SciSage 2025; DeepSurvey, DeepReviewer 2.0, and DeepSciVerify in 2026; 33 works dated 2026 in supplied queries) make the broad space partly anticipated rather than untouched. However, having multiple distinct frontier model families (Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.2 Sol, Gemini 4 Carbon) capable of strict schema-bound execution only recently made true cross-family institutional checks—integrated end to end with local computation (analyze, simulate), verbatim-grounded verification, planted-defect calibration, and final claim-ledger reconciliation—newly practical as the field shifts from fluent text generation to auditable epistemic workflows.
factors.improve: Concede upfront that single-family multi-agent drafting and isolated post-hoc verifiers already exist (SciSage, DeepSurvey, DeepSciVerify), and position the paper squarely at the newly opened inflection point: end-to-end multi-family institutional separation of duties and machine-reconciled human accountability ledgers.

ideaReview.ceiling: If a reframed version of this work succeeds completely, four groups of strangers change what they do next: (1) builders of AI-assisted writing and multi-agent research tools stop deploying single-family agent loops that grade their own output and adopt monotonic skeleton-versus-improver state machines with cross-family verification, live fault-injection calibration, and reconciled claim ledgers; (2) preprint servers, journal editors, and peer-review platforms begin accepting or requiring machine-reconciled claim ledgers, deterministic production journals, and human sign-off sheets as auditable provenance alongside AI-assisted submissions; (3) empirical and biomedical researchers burdened by manuscript preparation and submission checks shift from manual drafting and citation verification to supplying data and reviewing scoped change proposals and sign-off items while retaining explicit accountability; and (4) HCI and science-of-science researchers use replayable multi-family runs to study human oversight across autonomy settings and empirically test whether pre-writing structural rubrics predict impact once network and positive-result biases are controlled.
ideaReview.summary: Galley's underlying software (@autonomio/galley 0.1.0) contains genuine architectural substance—a 27-step monotonic skeleton-versus-improver ladder, strict cross-family separation of duties, verbatim abstract-grounded citation verification with planted-defect calibration, and a reconciled claim ledger paired with a human sign-off sheet—but the paper as seeded fails the impact standard and must be reformulated before drafting. Its weakest factor is surprising_and_certain (0): multi-agent drafting and verification are partly anticipated by 2025–2026 prior art (SciSage, DeepSurvey, DeepReviewer 2.0, DeepSciVerify), while the seed's headline claims—producing papers with projected high-impact potential from a seed alone (C9) at thousands-of-papers volume (C21), offering human-controlled review workflows (C12–C15), and proving behavior reliability while rejecting extensive software test suites (C22–C24)—have no empirical validation in C26's N=1 autonomous self-run, especially since C1 leaves what drives impact unanswered and whether the seven-factor profile predicts citation impact remains unknown. The seed also scores 1 on shared_bottleneck (blocked-researcher headcounts are unknown and biomedical guideline compliance is mismatched to autonomous seed-to-preprint volume), conventional_body_one_graft (an HCI paper with zero human evaluation, anti-testing polemics, and multiple competing grafts), and cheap_to_adopt (six bundled ideas and multi-CLI/ecosystem coupling instead of one crisp noun and one portable pattern). Reframing around one testable governance idea—cross-family epistemic verification and reconciled claim ledgers—while demoting unproven impact claims to explicit hypotheses, dropping testing polemics, scoping human-loop controls accurately, and grounding claims in hard verification/calibration and comparative evidence can salvage a focused, credible contribution.

selectedDirection.reason: D2 preserves the whole-system introduction and centers it on an inspectable design rule. Galley assigns review to a different model family, checks citation excerpts verbatim, and records planted-defect calibration in a replayable journal. The autonomous self-run can demonstrate those mechanisms. Comparative error reduction, high-volume throughput, and citation impact remain untested.

plan.thesis: A semi-autonomous scholarly editor can be run from a raw text seed to a submission-ready preprint under a code-enforced rule that no model family judges its own output, across isolated, replayable atomic behaviors, with its reliability checked inside each run rather than by offline test suites, as galley's own unattended run producing this manuscript shows; whether such papers achieve high impact remains an open hypothesis.
plan.workingTitle: Galley: Cross-Family Separation of Duties and In-Run Calibration for a Semi-Autonomous Scholarly Editor
opens: A controlled comparison of cross-family and single-family verification and review on the same seeds, measuring how many planted defects each catches, how many false alarms each raises, and how often each accepts weak author responses.
Extending in-run planted-defect calibration from abstract passages to full texts, computed analyses, simulation results and figures.
A user study of galley's dial, @both proposed-change threads and sign-off sheet that tests whether authors check or rubber-stamp the claims and decisions the system added.

A forward-looking science-of-science study that scores papers on the seven-factor profile before publication and tests whether the profile predicts later citation impact once coauthorship-network position and positive-result bias are controlled for.

A seed-to-preprint benchmark that scores systems such as galley, SciSage, DeepSurvey and DeepSciVerify-style pipelines on seeds from outside authors across fields, using the claim ledger and the Resolvent evidence package as the shared scoring format.
Applying cross-family separation of duties to other kinds of evidence-bound writing, such as drafting clinical guidelines, legal briefs or intelligence assessments.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.purpose: Opens with the unsettled question of what sets high-impact papers apart and the gap between a valuable idea and a submission-ready paper. Introduces Galley and the package it produces from a text seed, states the thesis with downstream impact framed as an open hypothesis, lists the contributions as a true list, and gives the release.

sections.title: Related Work
sections.purpose: Places Galley among multi-agent systems for surveys, peer review and citation checking, provenance tools for AI-assisted writing, work on fabricated citations and on LLM self-preference, and the established practices of separation of duties and fault seeding. Identifies the gap that prior scholarly systems assign roles through prompts and state no rule that the evaluating model must come from a different family than the producing one.

sections.title: Cross-Family Separation of Duties
sections.purpose: Defines the paper's noun and the five decisions it governs, and gives the seat assignment of this run. States it as a governance pattern for evidence-bound multi-agent writing that needs at least three model families and a prompt-and-answer journal, and that works without Galley's other components.

sections.title: Architecture: Atomic Behaviors and the Ladder
sections.purpose: Describes the 27-behavior ladder and the scheduler that rescans from the top after anything settles, the split between seven required skeleton behaviors and improvers that cannot stop a paper, and the isolated, tool-less JSON command-line steps whose journal makes every run replayable. Records that the authors built the behaviors one at a time, each shown working before the next, carrying the atomic-behavior design over from autonomio/poise.

sections.title: From Seed to Verified Evidence
sections.purpose: Follows a seed through the seven-factor impact interrogation, the reformulate verdict with three structurally different directions chosen by another family, optional systematic review, data analysis and simulation on the authors' machine, and evidence search through Canary over OpenAlex. Specifies the verbatim-gated citation verification with its three outcomes and DOI-registry records, and how claims without evidence become hypotheses that reassess and fidelity act on.

sections.title: Cross-Family Peer Review and Reconciliation
sections.purpose: Describes the methods, field, citations and desk-editor referee seats drawn from non-author families and rotated between rounds, finding severities, the four kinds of author answer, judgment by the raising referee, and adjudication by a third family after the answer cap. Ends with the closing reconciliation in which a non-author family confirms, narrows or drops each ledger claim so that the ledger, evidence package and sign-off sheet match the final text.

sections.title: In-Run Calibration
sections.purpose: Argues that reliability is checked inside each run on the manuscript's own inputs, through code-enforced verbatim matching, planted-defect calibration and cross-family reconciliation, in place of long offline test suites. Specifies how calibrate mixes planted defective citations and unaltered controls among verified ones and the two rates it reports in the production record.

sections.title: Optional Human Control and Provenance
sections.purpose: Describes how a person can join at any point without being required: editor edits become their revision, comments become threads the agents take over, the person keeps (@humans) or both share (@both) as proposed changes, citation choices, and the dial. Then describes the provenance each run leaves: the claim ledger, the production record, the sign-off sheet of decisions only the authors can make, and the Resolvent evidence package.

sections.title: Evaluation: A Self-Referential Run
sections.purpose: Reports the single unattended run in which Galley produced this manuscript from the authors' seed, with its settings (autonomous dial, automatic citation, 2 referee rounds, an answer cap of 3, up to 10 candidate works per claim) and seat assignment. Defines submission-ready as Galley's own gates holding on one revision, and states every count and rate only as it appears in the production record generated from the run's journal.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.purpose: States once what the work does not show: whether Galley's papers reach high citation impact, whether Galley can produce them at high volume, and whether the seven-factor profile predicts impact, all held as open hypotheses. It also gives no comparison of cross-family with single-family review and no user evaluation of the human controls; outside systematic reviews it checks citations against abstracts only; and its evidence is one run, one seed and one assignment of families, with no baseline system.

sections.title: What This Opens
sections.purpose: Names the studies the work makes possible: a controlled comparison of cross-family and single-family verification and review on the same seeds, calibration extended to full texts, analyses, simulations and figures, a user study of the dial, @both threads and the sign-off sheet, a forward science-of-science test of the seven-factor profile, a seed-to-preprint benchmark scored on the claim ledger and the Resolvent package, and the pattern applied to clinical guidelines, legal briefs and intelligence assessments.

outline.style: Register: an arXiv systems paper in computer science (digital libraries) written for HCI readers who build AI-assisted writing and multi-agent LLM tools. Use plain, precise American English with short declarative sentences, concrete nouns and active voice. One idea per paragraph, with the point in the first sentence. Use 'we' for the authors. Describe the design in the present tense and the evaluated run in the past tense. Name the system 'Galley' in prose. Set the package name (@autonomio/galley 0.1.0), repository URLs and behavior names (extract, verify, calibrate, reconcile, ready, and so on) in monospace, lower case. On first mention give each model by its full name (Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.2 Sol, Gemini 4 Carbon), then refer to it by seat (author, checker, challenger, verifier, referee, adjudicator). Define each glossary term once and keep it: always 'cross-family separation of duties' (never 'model diversity' or 'multi-model review'), 'in-run calibration' (never 'clinical calibration' or 'live testing'), 'model family', 'seat', 'atomic behavior', 'improver', 'skeleton behavior'. 'Submission-ready' always means that Galley's gates held on one revision, never acceptance by outside reviewers. Give numbers with units or counts ('10 candidate works per claim', '2 referee rounds', 'a cap of 3 answers per finding', '27 behaviors'). Every count or rate from the run comes only from the generated production record, and the prose invents none. Use numeric bracketed citations. Cite only verified passages, and phrase claims without evidence as hypotheses ('we hypothesize'). Make no claim that cross-family review catches more errors than single-family review, and do not imply that the human controls were tested with users. Call citation impact, high-volume production and the predictive value of the seven-factor profile open hypotheses, and do not list the seven factors by name. The introduction's contribution list is the only bulleted list in the body. Captions are self-contained, and figures are referenced as 'Figure 1'. Avoid hype and filler vocabulary, rhetorical questions and addressing the reader. Say nothing about how the text came to be beyond what the evaluation section reports as the run. The claim ledger and the statement of production follow the closing section, and the body refers to them by name.
glossary: cross-family separation of duties: the rule, enforced in code rather than through role prompts, that no model family selects among its own reformulations, verifies its own citations, judges its own referee responses, adjudicates its own disputes or reconciles its own final manuscript
model family: a line of language models from one developer, run through its own command-line client; in this paper Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.2 Sol and Gemini 4 Carbon each belong to a different family
seat: a role in a run (author, checker, challenger, verifier, referee, adjudicator) held by one model family
seed: the text a person supplies, and the only input a person must supply
atomic behavior: a unit of work that reads the paper's state, does one thing and writes its result, without knowing which behavior runs next
ladder: the ordered list of 27 atomic behaviors that the scheduler scans from top to bottom
scheduler: the component that scans the ladder from the top, runs whatever is ready and scans again from the top after any behavior settles
skeleton behavior: one of the seven required behaviors (extract, plan, outline, draft, frame, typeset, ready) that make a paper exist
improver: a behavior that can make the paper better but cannot stop it
seven-factor impact standard: the seven impact factors against which Galley scores a seed before any text is written and the finished paper after review
direction: one of exactly three structurally different reformulations of the seed proposed when the impact verdict is to reformulate, each keeping the seed's explicit commitments
Canary: the component Galley uses to search OpenAlex and, when the authors ask, to carry out a systematic review whose findings are audited by an independent model
verbatim match: the code check that a supporting passage is copied verbatim from the cited work's abstract, required before any citation is accepted
claim ledger: the list appended to each manuscript of every claim with its kind, its standing, its origin (seed or system) and its sources
load-bearing claim: a claim the thesis depends on, so that its lack of evidence triggers the reassess behavior
hypothesis: a claim stated without evidence and marked as such in the text and the claim ledger

in-run calibration: checking the reliability of Galley's judgments inside each run on that manuscript's actual inputs, through verbatim matching, planted-defect calibration and cross-family reconciliation, in place of long offline test suites
planted defect: a deliberately defective citation placed among verified citations to test whether the verifier rejects it
control: an unaltered verified citation placed alongside planted defects to measure how often the verifier wrongly rejects a sound citation
finding: an issue a referee seat raises about the manuscript, with a severity and the decision it asks for
disposition: the author's answer to a material finding: fixed with exact edits, rebutted, stated as a limitation, or needs evidence
adjudication: settlement of a finding still disputed after the answer cap by the family that is neither the author's nor the referee's
reconciliation: the closing read in which a family other than the author's checks the final text against every ledger claim and confirms, narrows or drops each one
production journal: the stored record of every prompt and answer in a run, which a rerun replays without calling a model
production record: the account of what each behavior did in a run, generated from the production journal and included in the manuscript
evidence package: the run's claims, evidence and sources, written in the Resolvent format
Resolvent format: the format in which Galley writes its evidence package of claims, evidence and sources
sign-off sheet: the list of what only the authors can decide: declarations, claims the system added, claims stated as hypotheses, decisions a third family made, and skipped steps
dial: the setting that controls which steps wait for a person: none (autonomous), load-bearing citations and critical answers, or every answer
thread: a comment in the editor that the agents take over by default, that the person keeps (@humans), or that both share (@both)
proposed change: an agent edit in an @both thread, marked at its place in the document, which the person accepts or declines
citation choices: a setting under which each claim waits for the person to pick one of its candidate sources (a, b, c), let the system pick, or state the claim without a source
submission-ready: the state in which every one of Galley's gates holds on one revision of the manuscript, which is not the same as acceptance by outside reviewers

frame.title: Cross-Family Separation of Duties and In-Run Calibration in a Semi-Autonomous Scholarly Editor
frame.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) produce fabricated and erroneous citations, and LLM evaluators tend to favor their own outputs. This paper presents Galley, an open-source, semi-autonomous, multi-agent scholarly editor that turns a text seed into a preprint package through 27 atomic behaviors. It contributes cross-family separation of duties, enforced in code, not role prompts: no model family selects among its own reformulations, verifies its own citations, judges its own referee responses, adjudicates its own disputes or reconciles its own final manuscript. It also contributes in-run calibration, a diagnostic audit of the manuscript's own inputs: code requires verbatim abstract matches for claim-level citations, planted defective citations and unaltered controls measure the verifier, and a family other than the author's reconciles the final text against the claim ledger. Together they form a governance pattern requiring at least three families and a journal of prompts and answers. In one unattended, self-referential run on one seed, with no baseline, Galley produced this manuscript in {{run.hours}} hours with {{run.calls}} model calls across three families. Its final argument holds {{run.claims}} claims, {{run.claims_added}} added by the system, and {{run.citations_verified}} citations passed verification. The verifier caught {{run.calibration}} planted defects and accepted {{run.calibration_controls}} unaltered controls, rates confined to this planted set. Submission-ready means only that Galley's own gates held, and no person independently audited citation support or manuscript quality. The work opens controlled comparisons with single-family review; whether such papers achieve high citation impact remains open.

factors.name: input_not_output
factors.evidence: The manuscript delivers an MIT-licensed open-source system (@autonomio/galley 0.1.0, 27 atomic behaviors) that turns a seed into a typeset preprint package with a claim ledger, Resolvent-format evidence package, sign-off sheet, and replayable JSON production journal. Section 3 also extracts a standalone governance pattern—cross-family separation of duties across five decisions plus in-run calibration—that other multi-agent writing systems can adopt using at least three model families and a prompt-answer journal without Galley's full ladder. However, it delivers no shared benchmark or ground-truth dataset (leaving a seed-to-preprint benchmark to Section 11), leaves the relation between Resolvent and existing digital-library claim-provenance models as an unverified hypothesis (C49), and notes that external readers cannot inspect run artifacts unless authors separately release the paper's folder (Section 8).
factors.improve: Ship a public seed-to-preprint benchmark dataset with human-audited claim-citation ground truth and recorded journals, and package the three-family seat-assignment and in-run calibration layer as a standalone, framework-agnostic library decoupled from the 27-behavior editor.

factors.name: shared_bottleneck
factors.evidence: Reframing the seed away from general citation-impact prediction and onto citation hallucination and evaluator self-preference raises this factor from 1 to 2. Section 2 grounds the problem in verified findings that LLMs fabricate 18% to over 70% of citations or introduce substantive errors (Walters & Wilder, 2023; Misra & Udandarao, 2026; Linardon et al., 2026, where only 43.5% of 333 citation-claims were accurate) and that LLM judges favor their own outputs over equal-quality alternatives (Panickssery et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025). Anyone building multi-agent scholarly writing or evidence-bound review pipelines faces the problem of independent verification. It falls short of 3 because autonomous end-to-end preprint generation serves a specialized builder community rather than blocking most researchers directly, family-level (as distinct from single-model) self-preference is explicitly treated as an unverified design precaution (Sections 1 and 2), and abstract-only OpenAlex matching leaves full-text methods and results claims blocked outside model-run reviews (Section 10).
factors.improve: Establish empirically that same-family models share evaluation blind spots across distinct models from one developer, and extend verbatim and semantic verification from OpenAlex abstracts to full-text passages, tables, and methods where working researchers are most often blocked.

factors.name: conventional_body_one_graft
factors.evidence: Up from 1 before drafting, Section 2 situates the manuscript within recognizable NLP, AI-for-science, and HCI conversations—citing multi-agent scholarly systems (DeepSurvey, The AI Scientist v1/v2), writing-provenance interfaces (HaLLMark, DraftMarks, InkSync), citation fabrication studies, LLM-as-a-judge self-preference, and disjoint-family judge panels (PoLL)—while grafting engineering practices from outside AI writing. However, instead of one clean graft in pure host-field prose, the paper imports two separate engineering practices (organizational separation of duties from security and fault-seeding/mutation analysis from software testing), retains an unintegrated science-of-science opening on coauthorship network centrality (Section 1) alongside the untested seven-factor impact heuristic (Sections 5 and 10), relies on custom system vocabulary (ladder, skeleton vs. improvers, Canary, Resolvent, the dial), and leaves key host-field positioning claims (C28, C29, C46, C49) as unverified hypotheses.
factors.improve: Cut the residual science-of-science citation-impact framing and internal system jargon, verify the host-field gap claim (C29) against full texts, and center the manuscript on one sharp graft—organizational separation of duties enforced across model families—written entirely in the LLM-evaluation and scholarly-workflow idiom.

factors.name: surprising_and_certain
factors.evidence: Remains at 0 because none of the factor's three conditions—improbable beforehand, undeniable afterwards, holding up in strangers' hands—is met. Given prior end-to-end AI paper generators (Lu et al., 2024; Yamada et al., 2025) and disjoint-family evaluator panels (Verga et al., 2024), enforcing family disjointness in orchestrator code and checking verbatim abstract substrings is straightforward engineering rather than improbable beforehand. Afterwards, the core governance claim is empirically untested: evaluation rests on one unattended self-referential run on one seed with one seat assignment, no baseline, and 'submission-ready' defined tautologically as Galley's own internal gates holding (Sections 1, 9, 10; C26, C42). No experiment tests whether cross-family separation catches more errors than single-family review; calibration tested only 6 planted defects and 2 already-accepted controls (measuring consistency with an earlier judgment rather than accuracy, Section 7); no human audited the 23 verified citations, 76 resolved findings, or final text-to-ledger reconciliation (Section 10); and because the seed describes Galley itself, 26 of the 44 ledger claims (25 'the authors' own work' plus 1 'premise') needed no external evidence, while 4 of the 18 external claims—including the novelty gap claim C29—ended as unverified hypotheses.
factors.improve: Execute the 3x3 journal-replay experiment described in Section 11 (crossing producer and judge families, plus same-model vs. distinct-model pairings within families), run multiple non-self-referential seeds in strangers' hands, and have blinded human annotators audit claim-citation accuracy, planted/natural defect recall, and manuscript quality against a single-family baseline.

factors.name: opens_more_than_closes
factors.evidence: Section 11 outlines six concrete, well-specified follow-up studies: a 3x3 cross-family versus single-family replay experiment using stored journals, fault-seeding calibration extended to full texts/analyses/simulations/figures, an HCI study of the autonomy dial and @both proposed-change threads and sign-off sheets, a prospective citation test of the seven-factor profile, a shared seed-to-preprint benchmark, and domain transfer to clinical guidelines, legal briefs, and intelligence assessments. Deterministic journal replay and open-source MIT code give researchers practical hooks for these studies. However, it stays at 2 rather than 3 because Study 1 is the foundational validation of Galley's own core premise; until the paper proves cross-family separation and in-run calibration actually reduce real errors, few outside groups will invest papers extending the architecture, and run folders are not publicly hosted by default (Section 8).
factors.improve: Complete the foundational cross-family versus single-family validation inside this paper so follow-up work builds on an established effect, and publish an open archive of recorded production journals and diverse seeds that external researchers can replay and benchmark immediately.

factors.name: cheap_to_adopt
factors.evidence: Up from 1 before drafting, the manuscript coins usable labels ('cross-family separation of duties' and 'in-run calibration') and explicitly isolates a standalone governance pattern in Section 3 that requires only at least three model families (so adjudication avoids both author and referee families) and a prompt-answer journal, making the rule conceptually portable to clinical, legal, or intelligence writing outside Galley (Section 11). It stops short of 3 because the title and contributions still bundle two multi-part mechanisms alongside a 27-behavior editor rather than one atomic idea, adopting the rule operationally requires configuring and paying for CLI access across at least three separate frontier model providers, and the reference code ships as a full scholarly editor rather than a minimal plug-in module.
factors.improve: Focus the contribution on a single portable rule and release a minimal, standalone cross-family governance and fault-seeding module that wraps standard LLM client calls in a few lines of code without requiring the 27-behavior Galley workflow.

factors.name: early
factors.evidence: Multi-family orchestration of long-horizon drafting and review became practical only recently with multiple distinct frontier model families (Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.2 Sol, Gemini 4 Carbon in this run) alongside open scholarly indexes like OpenAlex (Priem et al., 2022, 2024). Nearly all host-field references on autonomous paper writing, citation hallucination, LLM judge bias, and AI writing provenance date from 2023 to 2026, showing that governance norms for agentic science are still unsettled. It scores 2 rather than 3 because end-to-end autonomous paper generators (The AI Scientist v1 in 2024 and v2 in 2025), citation-alignment survey agents (DeepSurvey, 2026), provenance editors (HaLLMark, InkSync, DraftMarks), and disjoint-family evaluation panels (PoLL, 2024) have already opened the space, placing Galley in the second-wave reliability/governance phase rather than first-mover territory.
factors.improve: Apply cross-family separation and in-run fault seeding to an earlier-stage capability frontier where multi-agent governance does not yet exist, such as autonomous verification of computational reproductions, formal proofs, or raw experimental artifacts.

profileAfter.ceiling: Capped at a niche engineering demonstration or workshop-level systems note because the multiplicative standard sinks any paper with a near-zero factor, and surprising_and_certain remains 0. Without a baseline comparison, external seeds, or independent human audit, readers can cite Galley only as an existence proof of multi-family orchestration rather than an established reliability result. Raising surprising_and_certain to 2 or 3 via controlled cross-family versus single-family experiments with human-audited accuracy on non-self-referential seeds would lift the ceiling to a durable governance and methodology reference for multi-agent scholarly and evidence-bound AI systems.
profileAfter.summary: Compared with the pre-drafting seed (2, 1, 1, 0, 2, 1, 2), the finished manuscript raises shared_bottleneck, conventional_body_one_graft, and cheap_to_adopt from 1 to 2 by recentring on citation fabrication and evaluator self-preference, grounding Related Work in 23 verified OpenAlex citations across five literature streams, and extracting a standalone three-family governance pattern alongside an MIT-licensed codebase. However, surprising_and_certain remains at 0—and under a multiplicative standard where one near-zero factor sinks a paper, the manuscript should be reformulated rather than sent out as-is. To stay faithful to its evidence, the run narrowed its thesis to a tautological internal existence claim ('submission-ready under its own gates' on one self-referential seed with no baseline and no human audit), where 26 of 44 ledger claims needed no external evidence as the authors' own work or premises, 4 of 18 external claims (including the core gap claim C29) ended as unverified hypotheses, and calibration checked only 6 planted defects and 2 previously accepted controls. Reframing the paper around the controlled 3x3 cross-family versus single-family replay experiment proposed in Section 11—evaluated on external seeds with blinded human audits while trimming residual science-of-science and system-tour sprawl—is needed to convert an honest architectural demonstration into a surprising, certain empirical contribution.
